On the Orders of the Day:
Mr. PAMPHILE REAL DuTREMBLAY (Laurier-Outremont) :	Before the Orders
of the Day are called, I should like to know, in view of the situation in Europe at the present time between the Allies and Germany, whether the Government intends to take proper steps to ensure the indemnity which Canada was supposed to be entitled to, or which, at hny rate, we hoped to receive from Germany.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no statement I can
make just now having particular reference to reparations, other than such as applies to the general question of reparations, which of course is in the hands of the Supreme Allied Council. This matter was referred to yesterday in more general terms by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) when enquiry was made whether a statement could not be given to the House as to the condition of affairs consequent upon the demand for distinct reparation proposals from Germany by that Supreme Council, and the unsatisfactory response thereto. As I said yesterday, continual communication passes between the British Government and ourselves as to the principal occurrences of the Supreme Allied Council. Those communications are marked "Secret", but I see no objection to stating in the House such of them as in certain form have already reached the press. The only result will be of course to give something in the nature of official confirmation to these facts. It will be remembered that the
41 i
Supreme Allied Council met, in January last, in Paris, in order to formulate proposals for submission to Germany on the question of reparations. An adjournment was made to London, and the meeting there took place last week. The proposals which Germany was asked to make were not at all as to the amount of reparations but rather as to the methods by which she should undertake to make good the call for reparations. At such meeting in London Germany undertook to lay a statement of her methods before the Supreme Allied Council, but she added thereto, or made a part thereof, proposals as to the amount of reparations as well, which, in the judgment of the Council, were not only wholly inadequate but constituted a challenge to the foundation of the Treaty itself; in a word, an intimation that it was not the intention of Germany to abide by the terms of the Treaty. That being the case, Germany was informed through the British Prime Minister that there was nothing in her proposals that could form even a basis for discussion and that she would be advised as to what steps would be taken in order to enforce the provisions of the Treaty itself. Consequently, Germany was advised, in . brief, as follows: First, that a small area on the right bank of the Rhine would be occupied; second, that it was intended to deduct from moneys owing Germany from outside countries for German goods a certain proportion applicable to the Reparations Account; and third, that control would be taken of the customs in all occupied territory. These intentions were submitted to the German representatives and, failing any adequate proposals on their part up to noon of yesterday, the Allied proposals became operative at that hour. It will be observed that there is nothing in the programme which involves an increase of the forces now occupying German territory for its enforcement and, as well, that no Canadian troops are engaged. I do not feel that there is anything more than I can say at the present time, except that no specific proposal as to cooperation is before us.
On the Orders of the Day:

In view of the very widespread prevalence of typhus fever in Eastern Europe, and in view also of the fact that within the last day or two cases of the disease have been

found among immigrants arriving at the ports of Boston and New York, I would ask the Minister of Immigration and Colonization to state to the House what precautions are being taken to prevent the introduction of this disease into Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. CALDER (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) :
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not
aware of all the details of the situation, but I can assure the House that every precaution is being taken at the present time to prevent the introduction into Canada not only of typhus but of one or two other epidemic diseases that are very prevalent in certain parts of Europe at the present time. As a matter of fact the countries of Western Europe are all keenly alive to the situation-that is to say, Great Britain, France, Italy, Spain and other nations-and they are taking every precaution to prevent the spreading of these diseases from Eastern to Western Europe. As far as my information goes there are but few cases of typhus at present at the quarantine stations at Boston and New York-very few cases. Only one case-which is located at Massena, in New York State-has broken loose. That case is under strict observation, and every precaution is being adopted to prevent the disease from spreading further. I may also state that we have stationed three of our officers at New York to study the conditions there and make themselves thoroughly acquainted with the steps being taken by the American authorities to prevent the spread of these diseases in the United States. In addition to that our own officers are very keenly alive to the situation and very strict instructions have been issued to the officers in our own ports to exercise every vigilance. At the present time not a single case of this disease has landed at any port in Canada and, as I have already said, very few in the United States. I can assure the hon. gentleman and the House that the officers of the Health Department are thoroughly alive to the importance of taking every means to prevent these diseases from entering Canada, and are co-operating to that end with the American authorities and our Provincial Health Officers.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I explained to the House
when this matter was up last it is my intention, when we get into committee, to propose amendments to the definition of a Canadian National as set forth in the Bill. As that definition constitutes practically the entire Bill, I quite recognize the importance of the changes which I have in contemplation. I have asked to have the Bill as proposed to be amended printed and

circulated, and I believe that has been carried out. I was informed this morning that it had been printed, and last evening I handed to the leader of the Opposition a number of copies of the Bill as proposed to be amended. I trust that under those circumstances there has been opportunity for hon. gentlemen to take communication of the amendments. Upon what may be called the principle of the Bill, it seems to me that very little is called for beyond the explanation which was given at the first reading. What needs to be clearly understood at the outset-I think it is perhaps scarcely necessary for me to mention this, but it is well to avoid any misapprehension-is that the Bill does not contemplate to in any way affect the status or position of any Canadian as a British subject. Notwithstanding its enactment we shall all remain, of course, British subjects; and under the definition as proposed nobody will be a Canadian national who is not a British subject. But the purpose of the Bill is to define a particular class of British subjects who, in addition to having all the rights and all the obligations of British subjects, have particular rights because of the fact that they are Canadians. I think we have always understood that without a specific statutory definition there has for a long time been such a person as a Canadian, and some outstanding indications which justify a man in claiming to be a Canadian. But we have reached a stage now where there are certain specific rights created in favour of Canadians, or, to use the expression in the Bill, of Canadian nationals, as such, and should the legislation which this House last year asked to have passed by the British Parliament clearing up any doubt as to the extra-territorial effect of our legislation be enacted, as I have every reason to believe it will be, it will then be important to have a clear-cut definition of who are the people who may be affected by that legislation.
I might give an outstanding instance of where we have rights created in favour of Canadian nationals the provisions of the Convention establishing the permanent Court of International Justice. Under those provisions-which I have no doubt will meet with the approval of this House when the Convention is brought down- the judges of that court are to be elected by the representatives of the different members of the League. To secure election, it is essential that a candidate or aspirant should have a majority of the votes both
of the Council and of the Assembly. Each country, member of the League, has a right, -a right not to be exercised directly by its government, but in the manner which I will point out in a moment-to nominate candidates. Each country proceeding in the manner to which I have referred is entitled to nominate four candidates; not more than two, however, of those candidates can be Nationals of the nominating country. So there we have a case where we need to distinguish between a National and a nonNational of the nominating country.

Will the minister allow me a question? He states that a distinction has to be made between a Canadian national and a Canadian citizen. Is it on account of the League of Nations that the word "national" is used?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have already a definition of a Canadian citizen in the Immigration Act, but that definition is expressly limited to the Act itself, and we have no definition of a Canadian citizen which can be of general application.

That is not exactly
what I had in my mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I know, but I wanted to make that clear. There is a reason for using the word "national" rather than the word "citizen." It is to be found in this, that in the particular convention to which I referred and in the general proceedings of the League the word "national" is used as designating a person, whether subject or citizen, who forms part of the people of a particular member of the League. I am not certain that "national" is perhaps the most desirable word for England, but the word used in the French version of those proceedings by which the word "national" in our Bill should be translated is the word "ressortissant." I think the idea of using that word was to avoid the necessity of making distinctions between people who are subjects or citizens of a country and to get one word that, whatever the national designation, would cover the class of people who constitute the people of that country.
M. BUREAU: Le mot "ressortissant,,r est-il celui employe dans les procedures officielles de la Societe des nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Oui, le mot est celui employe. But perhaps I had better proceed in English. In the official documents this word "ressortissant" is used. You may have to talk of the "subject" of one country

and of the "citizen" of another country, but in "ressortissant" you get one word for them all. We passed considerable time with some very distinguished French gentlemen and some equally distinguished English gentlemen trying to find an English word that would be an exact translation of "ressortissant."
Do they use the word "national" in the English translation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, the word "national" is taken as the translation of the word "ressortissant." It seems further desirable that in making the definition we should use the term which is employed in these documents, because, after all, what we want to do, so far as that is a particular reason for this measure, is to have a clear-cut definition of who is the person who, as being a national of Canada, is entitled to these rights.
There is to be found in the convention a further reason for having this clear-cut definition. There is a provision in the convention that if two or more candidates, nationals of the same member of the League, should be elected judges, the question of which of these should be the judge is to be determined-and it is perhaps consoling to those of us who are not as young as we at one time were-in favour of the gentleman who counts the largest number of years to his credit. But it is obviously important that we should be able to establish just who is a Canadian national, so that it may not be suggested that, if another British subject is elected and one of our men is elected, that would be a case of the election of two men who are nationals of the same member of the League. I may say that the convention as originally drafted might have been open to that suggestion, but at the instance of the representatives of Canada, among others, the wording was modified so as to make it quite clear that this question of one giving way to the other would not arise when there were elected not merely two nationals of the British Empire, but two nationals of the same member of the League. That is another instance in which we have the creation of a right in favour of the Canadian national. The recognition that each member of the League has nationals of its own being once made so clear, it seems to me only a natural thing, even if there were no other reason for it, that this country should take the responsibility of defining who its nationals are, and that is

what this Bill proposes to do. As I said at the outset, there is no question of modifying in any way the position and status of us all as British subjects. The purpose of the Bill is only to define a particular class of British subjects-a class who have the peculiar quality of being that kind of British subjects who are nationals of Canada. As to the details, I assume we would deal with them better in committee. But speaking in a general way, if hon. gentlemen will look at the Bill they will see that the provisions defining "Canadian national", in the first place make such a Canadian national every British subject who come swithin the definition of a Canadian citizen under the Immigration Act. In addition, a provision is made with regard to certain classes of persons which follows the principles upon which the question of the quality of British subject is determined by the British Nationality Act, which we also have enacted. ( The definition of "Canadian citizen" in the Immigration Act limits the quality, so far as that quality results from birth, to the person born in Canada. In addition to the person born in Canada this Bill proposes to enact that the son of a Canadian national born while his father is a Canadian national, even though he be born outside of Canada, shall be a Canadian national. All hon. gentlemen will agree that if any one of us found himself in the unfortunate position of being absent from Canada temporarily with his family at a time when a child was born to him, he would want that child to be as full-fledged a Canadian as he is himself.
There is also a provision that the wife of a Canadian national shall be a Canadian national. With regard to persons such as the child in question, whose quality of Canadian national results from the fact of his paternity, though he was born elsewhere, there is a provision analogous to that which is found in the British Nationality Act, conferring uppn such a child, if he should be entitled to nationality in any other British dominion, the privilege of renouncing his Canadian nationality. There is no need of providing for what will happen if he is entitled to become and desires to become the subject of some other country, because that is already covered in the British Nationality and* Naturalization Act. Of course, if a man ceases to be a British subject he necessarily ceases to be a Canadian national.

In the case of men who were naturalized while they were minors, because of the fact that their fathers were naturalized, but who under the present Franchise Act have no vote unless they obtain a voting certificate-are they considered Canadian nationals under this Bill, even if they have not that certificate?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Anybody who is a
British subject and who was born in this country or who has domicile in this country as described in the Immigration Act, is a Canadian national. This proposed legislation, of course, has nothing to do with the franchise. I do not know what action may be taken in the future; the franchise may or may not be granted to all Canadian nationals, that depends upon the legislation of this Parliament on the question of the franchise. The Bill does not deal with any particular rights that are to belong to Canadian nationals; it is concerned simply with the making of a definition. The question as to what rights should belong to them or whether there should be differences between different classes, either as to the franchise or as to any other matter, is a thing that would have to be dealt with in separate legislation.
There is also provision for the case where a child is by reason of his birth a Canadian national, but by reason of his parentage or for some other reason, may at the time of his birth or later become entitled to recognition as a national of some other part of the Empire; the same privilege' is given to him to make the declaration whereby he would cease to be a Canadian national. Both these classes' follow absolutely the principle laid down with regard to the quality of British subject in the Act dealing with British nationality.
I would like to ask the minister another question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Might I suggest that questions will come more regularly and could be better dealt with when we go into committee on the Bill? Of course, I am precluded now from saying anything more on this reading save by way of reply to close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that,
from my point of view, with which all may not agree, this is another step in the wrong direction. When a false step is taken, it leads to another false step, and
the first one having been taken, the second, perhaps, becomes unavoidable, and that is possibly the situation to-day. The word "National", as a noun, would be properly and fairly interpreted in the language of international affairs as a citizen of a sovereign State. Hitherto, we have all been glad to be British nationals. Canada is not a sovereign State; I do not want it to become a sovereign State, and I claim the expression "Canadian national" is rather difficult to be understood. This is, however, a step in the wrong direction;
I do not expect to correct it, and I am satisfied simply to express my opinion.

speakeroldname: Hon. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
if I understand aright the explanation of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), this legislation has become necessary in order to define membership in the League of Nations. The word "ressortissant", which has been translated by "national", must mean that a man, although not, as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has stated, a member of an independent nation or of a sovereign State, has a voice in the League of Nations and must be more particularly identified. That is the reason why the expression "Canadian national" is used to translate the word "ressortissant", to show that the man belongs to one of the Dominions, that is, Canada. This Act on the statute books comes, comme un cheveu sur la soupe, an Act to define Canadian nationals. Might I suggest that, in order to facilitate the understanding of this legislation in the future, we put a preamble to it, stating in as few words as possible the explanation which has just been given by the Minister of Justice? I might suggest these words:	That whereas it
has become necessary, for the purpose of the better working of the League of Nations where Canada has a voice as a separate entity to define the status of the members who appear in the League of Nations as representing Canada, this legislation should be enacted defining these representatives as Canadian nationals -comme ressortissant de la nation cana-dienne, comme bon semblera. In that way, it will be seen in years to come why this legislation was enacted. In a few years the world will, perhaps, become normal again, and the next generation or the generation succeeding that will possibly be at a loss to know how this legislation came on the statute book unless some explanation is given by the preamble.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. member
will allow me, I am afraid he is reading from the Bill as it was originally introduced.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I explained the matter and I am responsible for the confusion. I am surprised we have not the Bill before us as reprinted, because I gave most special instructions and it was reported to me early this forenoon-
(Translation.) I am surprised myself but can we continue the discussion if we have not the Bill before us?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: (Translation.) I said, at the outset of my remarks, that in case some hon. members would deem it advisable, I would not insist on proceeding with the Bill, but how could I possibly make such a suggestion?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am out of order, I am afraid, but I only want to make the suggestion that Questions of this kind seem to be questions that should properly be dealt with in committee. The difficulty is that I am being asked questions and I am not entitled to answer. If, when we go into committee on the Bill, any hon. gentleman feels that he is under a disadvantage by reason of this unfortunate accident, I certainly shall not insist on pressing the Bill through.
I submit we should not discuss a Bill that we do not have before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All right.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising now is not to take exception to the principle of the Bill, but rather to draw the attention of the Min-
ister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) to the form in which the Government is introducing its legislation. This is the second important Bill to which, after its introduction, the Government has presented an amendment much more substantial in its nature than the provisions of the Bill itself, with the result that we on this side of the House are expected to discuss a measure, the provisions of which we have not seen and with which we are not familiar. It is quite true the Minister of Justice last night presented me with a copy of the amendment he purposes moving to the Bill, but the amendment is a more substantial measure than the Bill itself. While I have been favoured with a number of copies, there has been no opportunity for members on this side to consider the matter, and, what I think is equally important, there has been no opportunity for the country tc become familiar with the measure which my right hon. friend has introduced. We should have some idea of the measures that are to be discussed in this chamber, and some opportunity should be given for public opinion to express itself before measures are finally passed through this House. My right hon. friend would be taking a course that would be in the public interest if he would have his Bill presented in the form in which he hopes it to pass this House. The Government might consider that suggestion as applicable equally to all future legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If I may be permitted,
I thought I had said, we shall say, at* least half a dozen times, that I did not expect hon. members to discuss the Bill unless they felt ready to do so. I made the most frank, candid and open confession that there had happened this error; that I acknowledged my responsibility and asked nobody to suffer in the slightest degree, and in the face of that complaint is made that hon. members are expected to do this, that and the other thing, whereas hon. members had been assured that they were not expected to do anything of the kind.
It is the practice to which we are objecting.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Let us get the whole mystery and see what the awful crime of this Government was. The imputation is that this matter was not given consideration. The trouble came, perhaps, because it got too careful consideration. Two drafts were made of this Bill,

and the unpardonable offence that occurred was that, when I was handed the draft for introduction, I was handed the first draft instead of the second. My offence goes to that extent and no further. I have acknowledged that members should have this Bill before them and that they should not be expected to discuss the matter without it. As to presentation, if the hon. gentleman thinks something is to be gained by that, I have no particular objection to take this Bill back and re-introduce it. But as a matter of fact, the Bill as proposed to he amended is printed in full, and if it is not actually in the hands of members, the responsibility is on whoever has charge of the distribution of those papers. Let me make this suggestion: Let the Bill go into committee, as I said a few moments ago, and if then it is not thought there has been opportunity for its consideration, I shall certainly not press that it be proceeded with.
May I ask a queston?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We must come to
some semblance of order in this debate. We are debating the principle of the Bill on its second reading, where hon. members are restricted by the rules to only one speech. Now we have had two or three speeches, and all sorts of questions. I submit that the debate ought to be adjourned, or else brought to a conclusion, one or the other. If it goes on, we must adhere to the rules.

Mr. Speaker, I have not yet intervened in this debate, and therefore I am in order in speaking now. I think we should not be called upon to discuss even the principle of this Bill, without having had it before us. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), with his usual courtesy, has said that he is prepared to do everything to meet our reasonable requirements, which is only what we would expect of him. We accept the evidence of this spirit of justice, and I would now move that the debate be adjourned and that we proceed to some other business. If I want to speak again, I shall have another opportunity.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL

speechtext: The House resumed the adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. McMaster for the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this order was called on a previous occasion I was making a few observations in connection with it. I have given the Bill considerable thought, and it appears to me there are certain objections to it.
In the first place, I contend that there is no demand for this type of legislation. I have carefully inquired, and I am not able to find any record showing that ministers of the Crown in the past have in any sense violated the ethics or the privileges of their office in the way sought to be remedied by this Bill. From that standpoint, I contend there is no need of the Bill. In the next place, it is unwise for this House to persist in introducing legislation where legislation is not required. Our statute books are perhaps filled now with numerous measures about which the public know nothing, which are neither observed nor enforced and which serve no really good purpose.
Another point I would suggest is this, that you are not going to make men honourable or good by statute. My hon. friend in this Bill purposes to surround the morals and the ethics of a minister of the Crown with certain regulations. Now I think it is a sound argument to advance, certainly it is a sound reason in law, that when you set forth in a law a certain restriction, it carries with it the suggestion that as long as you keep within the exact bounds of that particular stated law, you are at liberty perhaps to indulge in practices that otherwise would not be indulged in. You may prevent a man who holds a directorship in a company from being a minister of the Crown or compel him to resign his directorship, but you do not change his position as an-individual, as a citizen, as a member of the company, towards the Government in the slightest degree, because it stands to reason, that it certainly would obtain, that while a man might conform with the technical demands of the law, he would not 
necessarily conform with its spirit. He may resign his directorship but retain his shares and be in exactly the same position as he was before.
The ordinary ethics obtaining in this House in connection with the position of members of Parliament, and more particularly in connection with those who in years gone by have held the high office of minister of the Crown, are such that I think the public has been amply protected in the past, and I believe it would be wise for this House to recognize that fact and rather to rest its case upon a personal sense of honour than upon conformity with some rule laid down such as this. My hon. friend in this Bill is seeking to prevent any minister of the Crown from holding the position of director in corporations. It is desirable, I think, that we should have in this House representative citizens from every walk in life. We often hear the statement made that we ought to have more business men holding public office, civic, provincial and Dominion; that it would be a good thing for the country if the capable, efficient business men of the country took a greater interest in public affairs; and that we might in that event run the affairs of the country more on a business basis. I am not advancing this as my own view; I am merely stating what is currently expressed by a large number of persons. Now, my hon. friend is going to circumscribe the entry of business men into the affairs of the country, and I want him and other hon. members of this House to consider this question: Why should we prevent a man holding a directorship in a company from holding a position in the Government, and yet allow the chief counsel, the chief legal adviser, of corporations to fill such a position? Certainly if there is a danger-mark you, I am not endorsing this argument; I am merely stating it as inferred by my hon. friend the mover of the Bill-in a man holding a position as minister of the Crown who happens to be a director of a company, I submit that there is still greater danger in having in that position a legal adviser or what is known as a corporation lawyer, a man who is engaged particularly in that class of legal practice.
I would say that if the Bill were to be seriously considered by the House, it should be amended to include legal advisers of corporations. Now, that is only one argument. I go a step further and submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that if that argument is sound-and I notice my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) nods his head as

if he accepts it as sound-then the auditors of companies, that is, expert accountants who are closely identified with large corporations should also be precluded. Let us take, for example, the auditor of a large bank, or of a large commercial or industrial corporation doing business with the Government. That official would be just as likely to be influenced by the interest of the corporation as would an individual who was a director. Perhaps he might not be influenced to the same extent, but almost so. Then we might carry the argument still further; and as I explore this field of argument I find its ramifications stretch in all directions. Take a large corporation like the Toronto Street Railway, the Montreal Street Railway, or an important steel corporation-any of these large institutions that have a great amount of insurance, we will say. They frequently do business with one firm. They contract with an insurance firm to cover all their insurance, running into millions of dollars. Now, does any hon. gentleman mean to say that there is not just as much danger of undue influence in this case as there would be in the case of a director of a company? What I am driving at in this argument is simply this: first, that there is no demand for this Bill, so far as I can judge; and secondly, that it is trying to state in a meagre statute, what ethics shall control the actions of a man who happens to be a member of the ministry. That is bad, in my estimation. It is inherently bad, and there is no sound argument, nor is there any demand for such legislation so far as I can see.
These are some of the arguments that occurred to me in glancing over the Bill. I confess I have not had time nor opportunity to delve very deeply into the constitutional history of the British form of government having regard to this particular measure. But I do not recall any statute of this character, or any stated rule of this kind, set forth in any of the great authorities, Bourinot, May or any other, as a desirable thing even. Consequently I submit to the House that it would be very unwise for us to encumber the statutes of this country with an unnecessary Act which, so far as I can judge, can do no good and in all probability would simply serve to dull the sharp edge of honour and ethics as they now obtain in connection with public office. It may have been well for the hon. member to bring the Bill to the attention of the House so that this particular branch of parliamentary ethics might come prominently before
hon. members and thus serve to remind them of their high responsibility. In that respect it has done no harm; but I submit that it would be unwise for this House to adopt the Bill as presented by the hon. member.

My experience is that a great many men who are directors of corporations-I think the resolution refers to them particularly-hold very little interest in those corporations, being frequently appointed directors by reason of their general knowledge of business and their ability to serve the corporations of which they are appointed directors. The shareholders may consider them so qualified from their business experience and their integrity that they make them directors without their having any particular financial interest in the company. I have known many instances where directors held not more than two or three shares-enough to qualify them. So that the mere fact of a man's being a director of a corporation does not necessarily prove that he has any real interest in the business. The man who is really interested is the man that holds the shares or certificates, the stock of the corporation. I do not understand by the resolution of the hon. member for Brome that it is intended to shut out the man who owns stock in the corporation, but simply the man who is a director. I think that the great majority of men who have become ministers, so far as my knowledge goes, have resigned as directors of corporations. Then again, there is nothing in the proposed legislation to stop a member of a partnership from being a minister; and a member of a partnership, whether it be two or four, is just as much interested in the business as though he were one of five or seven directors of a corporation. Therefore, the proposal, in my judgment, attempts to single out the director unnecessarily, and will

accomplish absolutely no good, because, after all, a man is interested largely according to the extent that his pocket is affected. Further, as I understand it, the independence of Parliament Act prohibits a man, no matter whether he be a minister or an ordinary member of Parliament, from being directly or indirectly interested -I think that is the wording-in any undertaking that has a business connection with the Government. In that way I think the public are amply protected if we regard people as honourable. If they are not honourable, you cannot possibly do anything by the wording of an Act of Parliament or resolution, to make them honourable-at least that is my opinion. The mere fact of this House passing a resolution or declaring by statute, that a director shall not be a member of a government will not-let me repeat-by any manner of means cover the desired ground if such person continues to be a shareholder, because, there is where his vital interest lies. I do not know why my hon. friend wants to introduce this legislation, because I believe that the present law protects the country amply, protects it just as well as it would be protected were we to pass the present Bill.

I am very glad to know that such was not the case. I have no hesitation in stating that I am a director of many large industrial companies throughout Canada. I am also a director of banks and trust companies. I ask how could it be otherwise? A man who enters business early in life, achieves a success, and becomes associated not only with a large industrial concern-of which he may happen to be the president, vice-president or managing	director-but with other
commercial undertakings in the city or town in which he resides, and who amasses wealth, will find himself invited to become a director of other large corporations, banks or trust companies. If a man is not successful in business, and if he is not possessed of good judgment he will not find himself on any of these various directorates. Now, suppose a business man is called to serve his country? It is 
a well-known fact that business men who have no desire to become members of parliament, great as the honour is, or to become members of a government although they appreciate to the full what that honour means. Judging from the political history of Canada and other countries it is a rare thing to find a business man, who has succeeded in commerce or in finance, either a member of the popular Chamber or a member of any particular cabinet. But, Sir, if the State does call that man, there is only one thing for him to do. He must place the duties of his public office, the duty of serving his country, before his business interests, and henceforward devote all his time and all his attention to the administration of those public affairs to which he has been called. If I may be permitted to make a personal reference for a moment my position as a member of the Government and as a member of the House is no different from the position which would be taken by any other business man. I had, of course, to drop all my business connections as far as my giving them any personal attention was concerned; I have not beer, able to attend to the duties of the various boards to which I belong. But, Mr. Speaker, is it fair for the hon.member (Mr. McMaster) to expect a business man identified with large interests in this country to at once resign from those boards upon his entering the Government? And after all, as my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has said, that really does not reach the kernel of what the hon. member for Brome is striving to accomplish as long as a member of the Government, or a member of the House, is a large stockholder in various large industries, banks, and other business institutions. Therefore it comes down to this: If one were to do what the hon. member for Brome desires he would have to throw all his stock holdings in various companies, on to the market and take whatever he could get for them,, resign from all these boards, and then appear before this House and in the words of the well-known hymn it would be a case of "Take me as I am". Surely no person who considers the subject seriously would for one moment expect a man who had been in business all his life to sell his holdings in these companies and to retire from these different boards. Because, secure as this Government is at the present time, as well as the party that sits to your right, Mr. Speaker,.governments come and

governments go. Therefore a business man would be most unwise to dispose of all his holdings and resign from all the boards on which he sat as a director in order to accept a passing honour in any particular government that might last for only a few years.
But, Sir, the vital point is the one I referred to a moment ago. Any Canadian citizen who has been in business in a large way and is a director of various companies, must put those interests to one side, and the honesty and uprightness of that man must be depended upon to serve the State rightly and to ensure that he give his full time and attention to the country's affairs. What difference would the fact make that a man had resigned from the boards on which he sat? As the hon. member for North Oxford has so well pointed out, as long as a man's interest remains in these various companies he would have the same interest in them whether he was a director of a board or whether he was not. Therefore I do not see the need or the usefulness of such a proposition as the hon. member for Brome has made to the House.
Let me say one thing more before I resume my seat. I do not claim to have any particular qualifications over and above those possessed by the ordinary business man for the position I occupy at the present time, but after acting for over three years as a minister of the Crown, and after an experience of twenty years as general manager of one of the largest corporations in this country, and having some knowledge of business, I have no hesitation in saying to hon. members that to be the minister of, we will say, any of the five or six large departments of government requires more business skill and more executive ability than to be the general manager of any of the largest corporations. I find no fault with so many gentlemen of the legal profession being in this House or in the Government; we need all classes of men here; but, Sir, if you are to have business men of large affairs in this House or in the Cabinet, then such small legislation as this, if I may be permitted to so term it, is only going to have the effect of still further discouraging business men from entering Parliament or the Government.
Therefore I have no hesitation in saying that I entirely disagree with my hon friend from Brome, and I am quite satisfied that when any man has the responsibilities of a minister of the Crown placed upon his shoulders he will see to it that he serves
the interests of the state first and his private interests afterwards.

Mr. Speaker, after having listened to the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne),
I have only these few brief remarks to offer. First, I think the minister, judging by what he has just said, is likely to be far more successful if he confines himself to building sailing boats than he will ever be by continuing to build a mercantile marine. The hon. gentleman has told us the number of companies in which he holds directorships, also the numerous companies of which he was or is general manager. This debate, Mr. Speaker, I do not think ought to be narrowed down to the personality of any member of the Cabinet, and I do not think it was the intention of my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMas-ter) to introduce a Bill which might be construed as being aimed at any individual member of the Government. The Bill brings before the House a matter of much higher importance, notwithstanding the importance that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine may have in the Cabinet. I do not claim that the Minister of Marine, because he is a director of many companies, is not a competent minister; and on the other hand I do not claim that he is a competent minister because he is a director of those numerous companies. Should a minister of the Crown have interests other than the interests of the state? That is the whole question. Several hon. members have addressed the House from the other side and they have told us that public life in Canada has shown numerous examples of ministers who had very large commercial interests and nevertheless served the state to the best of their ability. Such is the case, and I do not deny it. But, on the other hand, can you say, without danger of being contradicted, that our ministers have always acted in that way?
The hon. Minister of Marine has said that since he became a minister it has been impossible for him to give proper attention to his business interests. Therefore, I infer that as a director of the companies which he has mentioned he has not been of much usefulness to them. If he has not given any attention to those companies, why should he remain a director, why should he draw his fees? Why should he have any objection to resign his directorships if he has not time to attend to their business? On the other hand, if another member of the Cabinet is in the same posi-

tion as the hon. Minister of Marine, but, instead of giving no attention to the business of his companies, has done so since he became a member of the Cabinet, every hour and every day which he has given to the business of his companies is an hour and a day taken away from the state, and that attention and work devoted to his companies is attention and work that he should have given to the public business of this country.
The hon. minister asks:	Is it fair to
expect a public man when he enters the Government of Canada to resign his business interests when he may hold his portfolio for only a very' short period? That argument is commonly called the "Safety first" argument. I admit its strength, I admit that a minister when he enters a government, and especially a government like the present one, is not very sure of what may happen the day following his entry. But to keep in touch with his corporations and with his business associates as the hon. minister has to remain friendly with them, and should the interests of those associates diverge from the interests of the state, what is his position? The hon. minister has not explained that to the House. For instance, should the tariff policy be discussed around the Council table if the Minister of Marine is a director of several companies, and if those companies are interested in the drafting of the tariff schedules, will the minister think of the interests of Canada first, or will he think of the interests of his business associates? That is the question that the House is supposed to discuss. It is not a question of individuality or personality, although the hon. gentleman is very important in this Government; the question is away beyond his importance and reaches greater heights. The question is:	Are we to have in this Government
ministers who will be free from business interests so as always to make decisions in the best interests of the country at large?

make his investments in such a way, and should have business associates of such a nature, that neither his investments nor his business associations will interfere with his conduct of public business. That is my contention. I say further that a minister who is a director of a dozen companies and large corporations such as those mentioned by my hon. friend places himself in such a position that if he remains human, runs the risk of being incompetent, and if he wishes to be an angel he runs the risk of being misunderstood.

Mr. Speaker, it is somewhat to be regretted that the debate has taken a line totally different from that in which it proceeded in its earlier stages. It does seem to me that this matter should be discussed entirely free from personalities; that we should deal with the principle of the Bill and that alone. To my mind no real reason has been put forward in support of the Bill by its sponsor or by those who have spoken in favour of it. To me as a Canadian the public life of Canada has been, within my recollection at least, upon a very high plane; Canadian public men have held high and honourable positions, much to the credit of Canadian public life. But this Bill leaves the inference that a totally different condition prevails among our public men and in the public life of Canada, and it seeks to prevent something that has not at all become an abuse. In other words, its object is to prevent Cabinet Ministers who are directors of companies from working selfishly in the interests of the companies they serve as against the public welfare. In that respect I think the Bill is a reactionary measure; it is putting something forward to induce and perpetuate an atmosphere derogatory to the best interests of our national life. The promoter of the Bill has shown no reason why business men of wide experience should be debarred from the councils of Canada. There never was a time in the history of Canada "when men of great force, men of wide business experience, men of fine parts, men of honour and integrity, were more needed in the councils of a nation than they are to-day in this period of readjustment. What is the obiection to such men acting in that capacity? Is it any crime to be a man of business ability, of wide business experience? Should such men be debarred from the highest positions in the public life of Canada? I say, no; a thousand times, no. Not all members of the Cabinet need be men of these large parts,

but certainly the fact that they are men of that quality and of that class is no argument against their holding such positions.	_
It is contended that a man honourable in every way, without a stain upon his business, personal or public character, should not be eligible to hold office in the ministry if he be a director of a company. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) says it would ,be that man's duty, where he a minister of the Crown, to get all the business he could for the firm of which he was a director. But is it so, Mr. Speaker? Has the public life of Canada degenerated to such a point that the statement of the member for Guysborough is applicable to it? No. I rather take the view that a minister who is a director^ of one company or of two or three companies, if ordinarily inclined to be venal or corrupt, is much less inclined to be so in connection with his public office, if he holds a directorate, because he is under a fierce light; the finger of suspicion may be pointed at him because he is a director. His directorate is a deterrent force; it keeps him free from corruption and graft; free from any unfair activities on behalf of his firm. Let him cease to be a director, and what is the result? He has put on a cloak that shelters him, because he can say: I am no longer a director of any company, but I hold my stock; my influence is just as great in the councils of a nation as it ever was; I can get things done, and they cannot say that I did it because I was a director of a company. In other words, this Bill opens the door to the very thing that the promoter of it desires to prevent; it enables those who may be venally inclined to do the very thing my hon. friend does not want them to do by virtue of their directorship.
The Bill is filled with subject matters that might be carried a good deal further. Is the hon. member going to say also that if the member of Parliament happens to be a shareholder in a company he must be debarred from being a member of the government? It is as natural to say that as it is to say the other; in fact, if you follow through all the avenues that lead to interest it would not be long before you would have no Parliament at all.
My chief objection, then, to the Bill is that it reflects upon what I conceive to be a pure Canadian public life, and that it is put forward without any evidence being offered of its necessity. Surely, at a time when we in Canada are on the threshold of the readjustment period, with a
debt of $2,400,000,000 staring us in the face, we should call to the councils of the nation the best men we have from the point of view of business, from the point of view of the rebuilding of Canada, from the point of view of reducing the almost insufferable burden under which the country groans by way of debt. Public men honourable in character should be free from even the suspicion of attack that this Bill conveys. Let us get down to business; let us call to the councils of our country the best men we can obtain, and then let us treat them fairly and honourably, and be thankful that we get their services-services rendered, in many cases, at the expense of large personal business interests.

Mr. Speaker, I want to detain the House only for a moment or two in discussing this matter. Let me say, at the outset, that I am in grave doubt as to the wisdom of passing this somewhat drastic legislation. I am in that doubt because I would prefer to see a matter of this kind settled by what I venture to call the good sense, discretion and high-mindedness of men in public life, rather than by the strong arm of the law. There was a great deal in the argument of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) when he said that, as a pure matter of using properly the energies of a minister, it was necessary that this legislation should be enacted. We are all familiar with the old saying that "no man can serve two masters," and that is particularly true if each master wants all of a man's time. Clearly, a Cabinet minister's time is so much occupied that he probably has not time to devote to other businesses. One of my greatest friends in the press gallery when I first came to Ottawa said to me: "There is only one thing worse than being a member of Parliament, and that is being a minister," and I think, from the point of view of hard work, that statement was probably strictly true. Never having been a minister, nor having any particular expectation or ambitions in that way, I am personally unconcerned; but from all that I see of Cabinet ministers, their job is sufficient to use all their activities, so that the hon. member for Brome reasoned well when he said that if a minister's work is sufficient for him, if he accepts directorships of companies, he must either rob his country or rob his companies in the matter of time.
Then there is the further consideration that Caesar's wife should be above sus-

Mr. Speaker, it must be apparent to you and the hon. members of the House that the measure before us is not a party measure. It is in no way the policy of the Liberal party to attempt to do anything that will keep business men from taking their fair share in the work of carrying on the business of Canada. Every hon. member knows that John Smith, as John Smith, if he is a member of Parliament, cannot do business with the Government of Canada; but John Smith and Co., Ltd., incorporated, can go on and do all the business he likes. So I imagine what the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) had in mind was to create such conditions as would put incorporated companies on about the same basis as a man doing business under his own name or under the name of a partnership. But I submit in all sincerity to the hon. member for Brome that he cannot attain that object by the Bill now before the House, because there is nothing in the world to prevent a man, if he so desires, from withdrawing from a directorship if he becomes a minister and putting in as director his chief clerk or some other man in whom he has confidence, and doing business, and more business under that cloak which does not expose him to any legal attack. I submit that that man is

a greater menace to the state than the man doing business openly as a director, because in the latter case you know whom you are dealing with. Therefore, I am not at all in favour of the proposed measure. If my hon. friend were to introduce legislation that would prevent incorporated companies that had on their directorate a Minister of the Crown from doing business with the Government, I submit that he would be upon sound ground, but I fear the measure now before the House will be misunderstood, will do no good, and will not attain the object which my hon. friend desires. I am sure he had nothing personal in his mind when he introduced this measure. I am not going to offer him advice, because he is better posted upon these questions than I am, but it does seem to me that if he wishes to create such conditions as will prevent incorporated companies from abusing their privileges he might very well introduce such a measure as will put an incorporated company, with a director-in the ministry, upon the same basis as a private man doing business.
That is all I have to say in regard to this Bill. Looking at it purely from a business point of view, looking back over my experience in Parliament of now over twelve years, I am bound to say that the greatest menace to good legislation in this Parliament has not been the business men. There have been some other men who have been able to come to the members of this Parliament and go before committees, and it does seem to me that my hon. friend might exercise his energies in correcting some of these abuses before he attempts to interfere with busi-. ness men taking their proper place in the national councils in this Parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL

My mind on the matter is governed very much by considerations such as those put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), the only difference between myself and him being, I think, that I have advanced, or retrogressed, if that is a better word, to more definite conclusions than he.
The subject matter of the measure has no interest for me at all, personally. I am not now, and have not been for many years, a director of any company. I believe the Parliamentary handbook discloses my name as connected with two little companies in Western Canada, but I have to confess that they both went into liquidation about twelve years ago, and
I have not taken the precaution to have the Parliamentary handbook brought up to date. Possibly the House now has the explanation why these companies went into liquidation. Since that time I have not afflicted any company with the acceptance of a directorship. But my position with regard to this Bill would be just the same were I in a more favoured place as regards the business community.
I am not able to follow the arguments presented on behalf of the Bill at all. In the first place, this fact must impress itself upon the House: there is no other country that I know of, certainly none has been named to Parliament and the authority adduced, where legislation of this kind is in effect. I do not believe it is in effect in England. The practice may be in effect there of resigning directorships upon accession to Cabinet position more than it is in Canada, but I think I am safe in saying that that practice is by no means universal in England right up to the present time. In no other country is it in effect. It is not in effect in the provinces of Canada, nor has it been the practice in this Dominion to any great extent in all the years that have gone. Governments now existing and. governments that have existed, both in federal and in provincial affairs, have retained within their number men who still were directors of companies. Now that is a fact that, while it is not conclusive, must impress the House with much force. At all events, in the presence of that fact a considerable weight of argument would be necessary to convince us that we should mark out a new trail and impose new restrictions upon the accession to Cabinet position of men of business in Canada. We are called upon to do so by the mover (Mr. McMaster), and in very specific language by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), because of a principle which they claim to have discovered which compels us so to act. Now what is the principle? It is defined in different ways by hon. members who support the Bill, but in very broad language this definition is common to all: they say that a minister of the Crown requires all his energies and all his talents for his office; his master is the state; therefore, he should give all his time and all his energies to the fulfilment of his duties as a minister, and he should have no other interests of a fiduciary character or otherwise which conflict with the performance of his primary task. Well,



that is either a principle which we should follow or it is not. In the first place it is a principle that it is impossible to follow. It could not be lived up to as expressed; it could not be lived up to no matter how you express it. The hon. member for Dorchester says that a minister of the Crown should have no other interests at all to occupy his time. If that is correct, he should not even have a family.

speechtext: Oh, oh.
