I know that is an extreme interpretation of what he said, but it comes within the principle that the hon. gentleman argued for. What he asks for is that a minister's whole time should be given to the state, that the state should be his only interest. Certainly it follows that he should have no other interests of any kind, whether as director or otherwise. If it is true that where your treasure is there will your heart be also, then if his principle must prevail, one cannot have a treasure, one cannot have anything.
I was most impressed by the illustration that was given by the hon. member for East Toronto (Sir Edward Kemp). A gentleman comes into Parliament and is called to be a member of the Government. He i3 the owner or very largely the owner of a business. We will say it is unincorporated. Let us illustrate by figures, and say that this man is eighty per cent owner of that business. Now undoubtedly he is a trustee in so far as the other twenty per cent is concerned, in the management of that business, and consequently, he not only has his treasure there, but in a sense he is a trustee for others who have a treasure in the same business. Now we will assmue that he is called to public office as a member of the Government. He is permitted, if the Bill passes, to occupy just the same position in that business that he did before, and if he puts it into the form of a joint stock company, which would be a wise thing to do under those circumstances, he is not allowed access to the "treasure " that he has gained in all his years of hard work, to enable him to see that it is being managed at least fairly in his interests. He is not allowed that access that comes from the occupation of the post of director. He is compelled, merely because he has put that business into the form of a stock company, to abandon the earnings of his lifetime and to take no further interest in it than to commit it to others. He is not to be allowed to gain at least that access to, and that knowledge of, its super-

vision which he might have if he were permitted to retain the post of director.
Now, it is quite true that he cannot occupy any substantial time in the supervision of such shares as he may hold in a company by reason of his occupying the post of director. That is quite true. The fact that he is a director, however, keeps him in touch at least with his own investment; it keeps him in touch with the management of it to a certain extent; and without occupying any substantial portion of his time it there stands in a safer position, more satisfactory to himself, than it would be in if he were compelled to abandon it altogether and leave it to the management of others. Now, I am thoroughly in agreement with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that there may come a time when the occupation of high government office becomes inconsistent with the retention of directorships or with fiduciary relations to others; that time may come, but I do not think that its advent can be settled by legislation or that the severance can be enforced by statute. Indeed, that time has come in Canada. I well recall that the right hon. gentleman who occupied the position of Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) prior to the present minister (Sir Henry Drayton)- and so far as I know this is true of the present minister-resigned his directorships in all the companies he was in. He did that, I have no doubt, because of the belief that in the actual administration of his public office he came into too direct contact with the interests in respect of [DOT] which he was responsible as a director. There was such direct and intimate contact and relationship between his position under the Crown and his directorships that he felt it to be inconsistent with the proper discharge of his ministerial duties. It is to his credit that he took that position. There was a degree of intimacy and closeness of relation that does not at all exist ordinarily between directorships and the duties of a minister of the Crown. There was a directness of intimacy and a closeness of relationship which he felt made it impossible for him to hold both positions, and, as I have said, it is to his credit that he took that position, although I must say that I have not observed up to this hour that he was accorded any great degree of credit in this House or out of it because he took that stand. I did not observe that the hand of attack was

stayed or that the voice of calumny was stilled at all, because it was always asserted, with a random abandon that did not seem to me to be creditable, that he still was merely the mouthpiece of the business interests from which he came. However, he took that stand. And there have been cases in British public life where the same has been done; and I believe that in our own country public men of both parties on attaining office can be depended upon to see to it that if the retention of directorships in companies or even of stock in companies-because there is no great difference, if there is any material or imaginable difference between the relationship of a directorship to a minister of the Crown, and the relationship of a stockholder to a minister of the Crown- they can be depended upon that, if the relationship is so close that the administration of their office might be open to influence, they will drop the private interest in deference to the imperative demands of public welfare.
Now, I do not know how that may be defined by legislation. I do not know how it can be definitely stated when the time comes that the relationship is so close that the one position must be dropped. There is always a relationship. I do not know where one is to put his money if it is in a Canadian company-yea, or even if it is in an American company-so that it will be in such a position as not to be affected by any act of the Government of Canada or of Parliament. There is no place in which to put it so that it may be absolutely and entirely outside of the scope of the actions of Parliament. It is said that he should invest it in such a way that there may be no danger of his being influenced by it in the slightest degree in the discharge of his public duties. Well, I should like to have a suggestion as to how he could so invest it; personally I do not know how he could. It is a matter of degree. If one invests in any company or in any business in this country, whether he be a minister of the Crown or a member of Parliament, the destiny, the safety, the success of that investment is undoubtedly influenceable by legislation of this House and the administration of the Government. That you cannot get away from.
There is no fine and clear principle that you can state and enforce by the passing of this legislation. It becomes wholly a matter of degree, a matter of the good judgment of the man who is called to
public office. On that account it seems to me that this legislation would be futile. If you carried the attempt made by this legislation to the extent of the whole principle involved, you would be compelled to enact not only that a minister should not hold any directorships in this country, or exercise the slightest supervision over the earnings of his life up to the time he became a minister, and over the property that alone will be the support of his family when he leaves his public office, but that he must sell the stock he holds in companies that come into contact with the Government and with the administration of his department. And you would have to go further and enact that members of Parliament should do the same, because in the end it is Parliament that determines the legislation and not the government at all; and if it is feared that members of the Government will be unduly influenced by their holdings in various concerns, there is just the same reason to assume that members of Parliament will be similarly influenced.
It seems to me therefore that the House would be wise to follow the practice that has obtained in Britain, and in Canada as well, federally and provincially, and in every other country, so far as I know, and leave it to the sense of honour of public men and to the sense of accountability to the great public of the country; because in all things they do they are accountable not only to Parliament but to the entire country. Leave it to their own sense of honour and responsibility and we shall get better results in the end than by trying to enforce impossible enactments such as that put forward in the Bill.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL
speechtext:
I wish to direct the
attention of the House to the fact that the hon. member is about to close the debate.
Mr. DANIEL D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):	I want to
say just a word or two. The speech made by the Prime Minister is, in its conclusion, in direct contradiction to the speeches made by many of his supporters on the other side of the House. For instance, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) made a speech which was highly condemnatory of this Bill and of the principle which it espouses, and characterized the sponsor of it as a man who was usurping the rights and powers of Parliament and doing something that was entirely wrong.

That is not the way in which this Bill should be approached. Every member of the House, the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) included, must agree that the ideal condition is that a minister of the Crown should not be a director. That is the ideal. If one minister of this Government can be a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway, is there any reason why every other minister should not be a director of that concern? And is it a desirable condition, when the business of the country comes into conflict with the business of a private corporation of the magnitude and the far-reaching effects in operation such as the Canadian Pacific Railway, that every member of the Government should be a director of that company? When the question of rates came up, or legislation affecting the operations of that company in its relations with the people of Canada, would not the public be shocked to find that when the board sat as a board every member of the Government of this country was on it and that there was no one to represent the country at all? That is a condition that is quite possible according to the gospel preached by my good friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who launched into the hymn "Wash me and I shall Tie whiter than snow" and expressed other lofty ideas as if he wished to also have them set to music in this House.
Now I am not saying that this is a practicable Bill. I am not saying that it can be carried out; but I do say, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Brome should not be brought before the bar of the House and chastised and indeed brought to task severely, because he dared to introduce the measure. Its introduction has worked a lot of good. It has been shown that it was desirable, whenever it could be brought about, that members of a government should not be directors; that although we have fifteen or sixteen, perhaps twenty, heads of departments here, it does not follow that even although every one of them retired from being director of companies, anything would happen the country. In the event of their retirement the companies will go along just as they did before. The interests of the individual who happens to be a minister would, if he were not on a directorate, be in the hands of other directors, just as the business of other men formerly were in his hands, and things would go along first rate. Perhaps it is not practicable to carry out this proposition; but let me say to the Prime Minister as well

as to the House, that the ideal condition is that men who are ministers should have nothing to do with such companies in particular as are concerned in a large way with the Government.
The hon. member for East Toronto (Sir Edward Kemp) spoke about a private man acting in a private capacity, and that such a man can do business with the Government and be a minister; but the moment his business becomes incorporated he is debarred from serving in the Government or being a director of his own business. Well, those are small matters in a way. About a man who is conducting a private business as a manufacturer, or some other line, I do not concern myself at all; it is his private affair, and even if he incorporates the business the fact is still true to a great extent; but the cases I have particularly in my mind are those of any members of the Government who are acting in the dual capacity of directors of concerns that have to do with the public and at the same time are occupying positions as heads of departments that deal with these concerns. I think such a position is an anomalous one, and the exercise by ministers of such dual capacities should be avoided as much as possible.

Before the hon. member for
Brome closes the debate, I want to say a word or two on this question. It appears to me that the idea that the Bill may be passed in accordance with high moral ethics is not a businesslike proposition. The fact has already been referred: to that the business interests of Canada- and when I speak of "the business interests" I mean everybody who is engaged in any trade or commerce of any kind, which would embrace a very large proportion of our population-is now and always has been under-represented in almost every government that has been formed in Canada since I can recollect. That applies to the provinces as well as to the Dominion. Now this Bill which the hon. member has introduced would further circumscribe the bringing into office of any business man in Canada. It is well known that no man gets on very far in these days who does not become a director of some kind of a company. He might be a very poor director and it might be a very poor company, but he is a director of some kind of a company if he has got on at all in the business world. Yet this Bill would preclude him from taking his seat in the present or any other government. We now have in

Toronto a government that has not a single business man in it, and I am sorry for the province that it is so. If there were business men in that government I think some of the loans that have recently been floated at very high rates would not have been floated; they would have been placed on the market at rates that would have yielded a much better return for the money of the province than we are now getting. I say the same with regard to this Government. From time to time, I believe, the legal element has predominated and legislation,-often not very useful legislation-has emanated from legal men like my hon. friend (Mr. Mc-Master) who would like to pass his name down to posterity as the father of some [DOT] great Act in operation in the country. For my part I would like my name celebrated-and I have been here quite a number of years-as a man who has prevented unnecessary legislation from going on the statute books, rather than as a man who-had been a party to passing doubtful measures of any kind. There is far too much legislation passed in this country, and in my judgment it begets a contempt of law; in fact the people become so befogged that they do not know where they are half the time in regard to obeying the laws that this country has enacted. Many of such laws have gone through this House since I have been here. We let some through last session that members now are sorry for and they woke up to the fact afterwards. The truth is, Mr. Speaker, that far too much legislation goes through and in its passage it is hurried to too great an extent. My hon. friend from Brome has submitted a Bill that may be deemed perhaps to be receiving undue consideration, but it is a far reaching measure and it is quite opposed to the practice that has been in vogue in this country for many years. I believe if this legislation were to pass my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) would not have to resign from any directorates. I may be wrong but I judge that he would not have to resign from any directorates in order to qualify if this legislation were to pass, and that also may properly be said with respect to the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon). Holding the particular views that my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) does I do not think he would be a valuable asset to any ordinary manufacturing or commercial company, and therefore perhaps he is not so very much sought after. My hon. friend in bringing in this legislation is, I think, entirely in the wrong.
Let me say that I have known the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballan-tyne) for a great many years, long before he entered this Government. I have known him for at least twenty-five years and have done business with him, and I recognize him as one of the first business men of Canada. Now, to say that he should divest himself of directorates in companies because he is here to-day and-as my hon. friend would have told him last week- he is going to be gone to-morrow; he then called upon the whole Cabinet to resign immediately and get out, he declared-they have no place here-is unreasonable. The hon. member would compel a minister to divest himself of all his business interests, and in the second clause he calls upon him to do so within fifteen days after he is sworn in. Now a minister upon accepting office might go to his constituency and not be elected. He might have resigned all his business interests and thrown them to the winds, and still his constituents might not endorse him. Perhaps they would rather refuse to endorse him because of the fact that he had thrown away his business interests, and would no longer have that position of influence in the community that he would enjoy did he continue to retain his business interests,

because in every community the man who employs a large number of his fellows or makes a success of business is rightly looked up to. Are you going to put into office the man who fails, the man that cannot qualify, or are you going to choose the man whose business career has justified him in being selected among his fellows for a position of this kind?
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend has gone too far afield in this measure and that there is no call for such legislation in the Dominion of Canada at the present time. I do not remember the existing situation ever having infringed upon the rights of the people to any extent. I trust that no one in particular has been especially aimed at in this legislation. I do not believe the hon. member for Brome would do such a thing. I have a higher opinion of him than that, and I do not think he has any particular person in mind in the matter. But I would like to point out to him that his Bill would limit a class of men who may be selected for Governments, and it would cut out those who, perhaps by their training and by the success they have made in business career, are the best fitted for that particular calling.
I am not sure that my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar) who leads the third party was not

included in this measure. I rather fear he would be. While he has no doubt got his eye upon this proffered legislation and is able to look after himself, it seems to me that possibly the United Grain Growers and the Elevator Companies may be directly concerned. No one would say, no matter what opinion they had of the Grain Growers party, that the leader of the party was the man to be dropped, when it is doubtless understood that he is by far the most capable man for the position for which he has been selected by the Council of Agriculture, and by those who follow him.
I think, Mr. Speaker, when the House looks at this in a sober, clear way it will see that the interests of the country have not suffered, nor are they likely to suffer, because the moment any minister of the Crown showed that he was allowing his private interests to dictate his public policy, he would be a marked man in the House and in the country and the Government could not get rid of him too quickly. I hope the hon. gentleman will withdraw his measure, because I think it is pretty sure to be defeated.

Mr. Speaker, the reference to myself made by my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) induces me to participate in this debate very briefly. If I might be permitted a personal allusion, when the Union Government was formed in October, 1917, I held a directorship in the company with which I had been associated for many years, and I was also a director in one of the smaller Canadian banks. I am divulging no confidence, I think, when I say that before accepting office I discussed the matter with the right hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) who was then Prime Minister, and as far as my own business relations were concerned, it was clearly understood that my time was to be entirely free from them. As far as my position with the bank was concerned, I considered it then my duty to resign my directorship, and I did so.
I am in cordial agreement with what my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has said, and also with what my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) has said, that the best approach to a solution of this question comes through a high-minded sense of public duty. I am at a little difference of opinion with my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster). I cannot see that his position is entirely consistent or logical. He proposes that any

one who is a director of a corporation doing business in Canada shall sever his business connection on being elevated to the high honour of a minister of the Crown. If my hon. friend is consistent I think he must pursue that principle still further. Take the case, for instance, of a gentleman who may be elected to this House, and is the head, or a member, of an important legal firm. Should he accept a Cabinet position, would it not naturally follow, for the reasons stated by the hon. member for Brome, that he should sever his connection with his legal firm? We might carry the principle further. My hon. friend from Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) is, I believe, a general merchant in that town. If a new Government should be formed and my hon. friend should be asked to become a member of it, should he thereupon be compelled to dispose of all his business interests in Renfrew? I might pursue that line of reasoning still further, Mr. Speaker. My hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Reid) is a farmer. Were he to be elevated to Cabinet rank, would it follow that he should dispose of his farm holdings in order that there might be no division of interests in the prosecution and fulfilment of his duty as a minister of the Crown? I think that principle could be carried to very extreme lengths.
I do hold very strongly, however, that business of the Government should be entirely dissociated from the business of corporations of which members of the Government may be directors. I think that is in the public interest. After all, I believe the best solution of this question may be found in the development of the high sense of public duty that was manifested by Lord Grey in the instance given by my hon. friend from Red Deer. But the discussion has done good, and I am sorry that I was not in the House when my hon. friend from Brome, for whom I have a very high respect, introduced this measure, as I have no knowledge of what he stated on that occasion. But viewing the whole question on general principles, although I think it is very highly desirable that the conduct of our public men should be put beyond any possibility of reproach, yet it seems to me that the position taken by my hon. friend from Brome is perhaps a little too far in advance at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, in the observations which I made when introducing this Bill last Friday, I was very careful to endeavour to dissociate

any expression of personality in my discussion of its subject matter. I am glad to say that, with one exception, that attitude of mind on my part has been followed by hon. members who have spoken in this debate, and I thank them for it.
I am quite aware that there are arguments against my Bill. There is the weighty argument which has been discussed by the hon. member for East Toronto (Sir Edward Kemp) and by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb). Their point was that in the case of a man who has built up a personal business of his own under the law and the practice as at present there is nothing to prevent him accepting the office of a minister of the Crown and retaining his interest in his personal business-remaining its manager, so to speak. But the member for East Toronto said: If this Bill goes into effect, then such a man if he changed his business into an incorporated form would be precluded from being a minister of the Crown. Now, I had thought of that case before it was brought up and-I do not know whether I am exactly in order in making this statement, Mr. Speaker-in the hope that the principle of the Bill may be accepted, I thought of meeting such a case in this way: By defining what I would call a personally owned and controlled company. Let us define such a company as one in which 85 per cent of the capital stock is owned by the minister and his relations within the degree of first cousins, and the board of which is composed of a majority of the minister's relations within the same degree. Then I would make an exception of such a company and would allow the minister to retain his directorship; but if he did so I would preclude his company from doing any business with any department of the Government or with any national system of railways or of ships. I would be prepared to do that to meet the objection made by the hon. member for East Toronto and by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon, in which I think there is a great deal of force.
My hon. friend from East Toronto also said: Trust the ministers. That has been the motive, so to speak, of a great many of the speeches made against my Bill-that 4t is unnecessary and that we should trust to the delicacy of honour of the minister. If that is a good argument in regard to ministers, why is it not an equally good argument in relation to members of Parliament? Section 14 of the Senate and House of Commons Act sets out very
clearly that a member of Parliament shall not be concerned
-directly or indirectly, alone or with any other, by himself or by the interposition of any trustee or third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing any contract or agreement, expressed or implied, with or for the Government of Canada on behalf of the Crown.
The cases are not exactly analogous, but they are very similar. In enacting this legislation, Parliament in its wisdom has not relied upon the honour of members of Parliament. What the member of Parliament is told he shall not do are exactly the things which delicacy of feeling will prevent him from doing; nevertheless it has been thought wise to incorporate these prohibitions in the statute.
The next point to which I wish to refer was that made by the member for Park-dale (Mr. Mowat), whose idea was that Parliament should resent a Bill invading the realm of private honour-I think I quote his exact words. Well, this Bill no more invades the realm of private honour than the legislation we already have upon the statute book.
There is no demand for this legislation, says the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). I do not know whether the hon. member is apprised of the fact, but there is abroad among the people of Canada a very strong impression-to put it in the most moderate language-that the large business interests of the country now have and have had in the past, whether one party or the other was in power, a great deal too much to say as to how the country should be governed. The legislation which I am asking the House to adopt is for the purpose of preventing, as I said before, interlocking directorates from entering into the circle of the Cabinet.
The member for Vancouver Centre expressed the view that if such legislation as this were adopted the Bill should be extended so as to make ineligible for entry into the Cabinet a man who was acting as counsel for a large company. Now, that depends upon whether or not my hon. friend has reference to counsel acting under a yearly retainer. For instance, if a man acting as solicitor for a large company on the basis of a standing retainer of perhaps $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 a year should enter the Cabinet without resigning that position as solicitor, the procedure would be just as improper as it would be for a director to enter the Cabinet and retain his directorship. If I correctly apprehend what my hon. friend said, I am

perfectly willing to enlarge my Bill to that extent. I do not agree with him that auditors should be in the same position. The auditor, after all, is a man who sees that the books are kept properly. My hon. friend, who is not, I think, a member of the legal profession, should realize, as an intelligent layman, what a vast difference there is between the part played by the auditor in his connection with the company, and the part played by the lawyer as respects the advice which he gives. The hon. member also made a reference to including the insurance agent, but I think that was a species of humour on his part.
It is said, Mr. Speaker, that it is unnecessary and inadvisable to provide that members of the Cabinet shall not be directors in incorporated companies. But if I mistake not, it is specially provided in the Act creating the Railway Commission that no Railway Commissioner shall be a director in an incorporated company. Well, the cabinet sits as a court of appeal form the decisions of the Railway Commission; therefore we have this peculiar position: the court of original jurisdiction is forbidden to hold directorships, but the court of appeal from that court is allowed to do so. That does not seem to me to be logical.
Now, I come to the argument made by the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne). I may say-and I would call all members of this House to witness who heard me the other day-that in introducing this measure I studiously refrained from imputing any wrong-doing to any minister, and I refrained absolutely from making a personal attack upon anyone. But the Minister of Marine has endeavoured to attract the lightning upon himself; his doing so has been no fault of mine. The minister has been frank, if he has been anything. He said: I am a director in many large industrial companies, in banks and in trust companies. He seems to think that his holding of these positions is perfectly compatible with his being a minister of the Crown-and he now nods his head in token of assent. But, Mr. Speaker, he goes on to say this: The energy and the skill required in the administration of a large department of the Government is such that I have not been able to give any attention to my company matters-and he nods his head again. Well, in all kindness I ask him, is it fair to the shareholders of the Royal Trust Company that he should remain a director of that company, that he should give his name to the institution

and the prestige that his name carries with it, while he gives no attention at all to the aifairs of the company? Is it fair, is it right, for a man to hold himself out as a guardian of the interests of the shareholders and of the depositors, if there are any, of the Royal Trust Company, and yet give no attention to the affairs of the company? My hon. friend is a director, if I mistake not-and he will correct me if I make any mistake-of the Merchants' Bank of Canada. Is it fair or right that the workingmen of this country should be invited to place their hard-earned savings in the care of the Merchants' Bank of Canada, relying upon my hon. friend being a director of that institution, when as a matter of fact he tells us that he can give no attention to the matter? I do not think it is right, and I think that on further consideration, my hon. friend will come to the same conclusion.
Now, I do not want to make this a personal quarrel between the Minister of Marine and myself, because I have no quarrel with the hon. gentleman. But he has endeavoured to justify his retaining of directorships while acting as minister of the Crown. Let us return for a moment to the Royal Trust Company, which, he will admit, is a kind of side-door of the Bank of Montreal, or represents the same or almost the same business interests. Is it right that the minister should be a director of a company so closely associated with the Bank of Montreal as the Royal Trust Company when the Bank of Montreal is one of the bankers of the Government of this country? I do not think it is. My hon. friend may think it amusing, but there are members on this side who fail to see the humour of the situation.
In connection with this matter I wish to direct the attention of the House to an item published in the Ottawa Citizen of to-day, which states that Andrew Mellon, the new Secretary of the United States Treasury, resigned all directorships which he held on taking office under President Harding. I think that is the better method to adopt.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) endeavoured to push the matter to an absurdity. He wanted to infer that we wished to impose celibacy upon the Cabinet. We do not wish to go that far-that, I understand, would be a difficult job. I wish no longer to detain the House-
Hear, hear.

-and I am sorry if my remarks have caused such pain to

hon. gentlemen as to force them to give audible expression to what seems to me an almost discourteous desire to see me finish my remarks. There is no need for me to recapitulate what I said. It seems to me that the whole matter resolves itself down to this very simple proposition. The position of a minister of the Crown demands all a man's energy and skill, and I think that is one thing on which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) and I agree. That being so, if a minister retains directorships, he must, perforce, either neglect state matters or neglect company matters. I believe in most cases he will neglect company matters and give his time and attention to the state. That is unfair. [DOT] I have made no imputation of wrongdoing to anyone; but there is a possibility that there may be conflict of interest, and the public interest suffers. Even if that never happened, there is always the liability_ of the public thinking there is something wrong, and we should avoid that at all costs.

I	was paired with the
junior member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. R. H. Butts). Had I voted, I would have voted against the Bill.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

THE JAMES MacLAREN COMPANY LIMITED
Mr. G. H. BOIVIN, for Mr. Fontaine, moved the second reading of Bill No. 8, respecting the James MacLaren Company Limited. He said: When this order was called yesterday, the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) made some objections to the reference of this Bill to the Select Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills. I see that in

his remarks he stated that the Bill concerned the construction of railway terminals and telegraph lines, and that possibly it ought to be referred to the Select Standing Committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Since the order has been allowed to stand, the hon. member for Three Rivers has looked into the matter, and he has authorized me to say that he is perfectly willing that the Bill should be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and referred to the Select Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills.

subtopic: RESOLUTION WITH RESPECT TO OWNERS OF SURFACE RIGHTS WITHDRAWN

speechtext:
On the Order:
Resuming the adjourned Debate on the proposed Resolution of Mr. Griesbach. That in the opinion of this House, should oil be found and produced in or under any lands in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba, in which ownership to the sub-surface is In the Crown, the Owner of the surface right shall be entitled to one-si.xteenth of such oil, provided that such owner shall have made a homestead entry, or other entry, for the said land prior to the date of the application for the oil lease in the subsurface. And whereas, all existing leases contain a provision that they are subject to the provisions of the regulations in force at the time of the granting of the same and also any regulations subsequently adopted. Therefore alteration should be made in the regulations to give the owner of the surface rights a similar interest in the oil produced under leases heretofore granted in which no development work has been done upon the said lands under the said leases.

speechtext:
Mr. McCoig moves that I do now leave the Chair for the House to
[(Mr. Boivln.]
resolve itself into Committee of the Whole to consider the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the standardization of parts of agricultural machinery, and to enact,-
1.	That from and after the first day of
November, 1922, all agricultural implements and farm wagons manufactured in Canada for use * within Canada, shall with respect to the following parts, namely:-Grain Binder Knife Sections, Knife Heads and Pitmans, Mowing Machine Knife Sections, Mowing Machine Knife Heads, Mowing Machine Pitman's Clamps, Mowing Machine Guards and Guard Ledger Plates, Hay Rake Teeth, Land Cultivator Teeth and Cultivator Points, Sprocket	Chainsdifferent sizes, Plows Points, Plow Sole Plates, Plow Clevises, Ensilage Blower Pipes, Nuts for Wagon Arms, Machine Bolts and Nuts; be made to conform to the standards prescribed by regulations to be made by the Minister of Agriculture prior to the first day of November, 1921, and approved by the Governor General in Council ; and that further and other regulations may be made by the minister from time to time. "
2.	That from and after the first day of November, 1922, no agricultural implement or farm wagon shall be manufactured in Canada for use within Canada which with respect to the said parts fails to comply with the regulations then in force, and any manufacturer of agricultural implements or farm wagons for use within Canada violating these provisions or regulations shall incur a penalty of not less than S200 and not more than $1,000.

maintopic: STANDARDIZATION OF PARTS OF AGRICULTURAL MACHINERY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STANDARDIZATION OF PARTS OF AGRICULTURAL MACHINERY
speechtext:
I put the motion that
the House do now resolve itself into Committee of the Whole to consider the resolution. Does the hon. member desire to debate that motion?

maintopic: STANDARDIZATION OF PARTS OF AGRICULTURAL MACHINERY
speechtext:
I desire to say a few
words in connection with the resolution standing in my name. In the first place, it is very gratifying to be able to present to Parliament a resolution of a non-contentious nature such as this which I think will meet with the general approval of the people of Canada, including the manufacturers as well as the users of agricultural implements. I think the manufacturers of agricultural implements should be glad that such a resolution has been presented to Parliament, and particularly if it should be adopted. There never was a time in the history of Canada when the manufacturers were enjoying greater prosperity or higher prices for the goods they are disposing of to the agriculturists of Canada. This resolution, if carried into effect, would put them in the position of having many of the parts of their different implements interchangeable. The parts would be standardized so that if an agricultural implement shipped to a foreign market required a spare part, the purchaser would be in the

fortunate position of being able to get the required part from any Canadian manufacturers' agent which would not be the case with purchasers of agricultural implements from manufacturers in other parts of the world. This matter is not an entirely new proposal. It was up last session before the Committee on Agriculture, and in all fairness to the chairman and members of that committee let me say that they all recognized the importance of this proposal, and gave it their hearty en-dorsation whenever the matter was up for discussion.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that I was not able to advance the Bill I introduced in the House last session dealing with this matter, because it had not been preceded by a resolution, but I repeat, the members of the Committee on Agriculture discussed the matter, and one and all approved the proposal of having the different parts of farm machinery made in this country interchangeable.
For the benefit of hon. members who are not members of the Committee on Agriculture I might say that the first item dealt with in the resolution is grain binder knife sections. As you no doubt are aware, Mr. Speaker, all the sections are of exactly the same size, three inches, the only difference between different makes being that the holes are drilled differently, so that the sections are .not interchangeable; that is, one manufacturer's knife sections could not be used on the machine of another manufacturer. At present a man using a Massey-Harris binder who required a knife section would have to get it from the Massey-Harris repair man, whereas if these sections were made interchangeable he could go to the International Harvester Company agent, or the agent of any other Canadian manufacturer living up to these proposed regulations, and get the part he required. The same thing applies to pitmans. They are all wood, but they are made in different sizes, so that if a man breaks a pitman he has to get another part from the agent of the particular company that sold him the machine. The same thing applies to mowing machine knife sections. All the sections of the mowing machines are of the same size, but they are drilled differently. Then the pitman clamps are all of the same length, but they also are made just a little bit differently, so that they are not interchangeable. If this resolution were carried into effect these parts would be standardized, and then if a man wanted a repair part
he would not have to drive to the agent of the particular company from whom he bought the machine, but could get the part from any Canadian manufacturer of these implements.
If for instance a farmer broke a pitman clamp on his machine while in the hay field at a busy time of the year he would not have to drive to some dealer at a distance to procure the necessary repair. It is an article worth only thirty-five cents, but it is of very great importance, and if these clamps were the same for all makes of machine it would obviate considerable trouble and annoyance when time is of the utmost value. As it is, they are made just a little different in the various makes of machine and are therefore not interchangeable. The same thing applies to the knife heads on mowers. All mowing machine knives are made in five, six and seven foot lengths, and but for a little twist they are almost indentical; but this slight difference renders them uninterchangeable. Now, if this article were standardized a company would not need to reconstruct a mowing machine because the knife heads would be standardized and be made interchangeable, and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the resultant saving would be considerable, not only in money but in time also, which is of equal if not greater importance.
Another article which should be standardized-and this is of vital importance-is the ledger plate. The ledger plate has to be repaired from time to time during the lifetime of the machine, and I think it is highly important that a farmer should be able to procure this repair with the slightest possible inconvenience. This also applies to the hay rake teeth and land cultivator teeth. Let me say, for the benefit of hon. members who are not conversant with agricultural implements, that these teeth are of the same size, but they are slightly different in some minor respects and if a man wishes to buy teeth for a rake he may find that the ends of the teeth in one make are bent in the opposite direction to that of the rake he is using, and consequently no end of trouble and annoyance is involved. The standardization of this part of farm machinery could be accomplished without any expense or reconstruction of rakes; the expense to the manufacturer would be very slight indeed. This applies not only to hay rake teeth but also to land cultivator teeth. If a man owned a rake purchased five or ten years ago he could, if my proposal were adopted and these parts were standardized,

be able to go to some concern near at hand and get the proper repair.
The next article to which I desire to refer is the sprocket chain. I may say for the benefit of the uninformed on these matters that we could have three or four different sizes of chains but have them all standardized so that whatever number of chain a man wanted he could go to a repair house and get it without any trouble. The next thing is the question of plough points. We have in Ontario to-day five or six different plough firms making what is known as the No. 21 plough, which is the most desirable general purpose plough that can be procured. But the points in the different makes are not identical; there is just enough difference in the way the holes are drilled to prevent their being interchanged. All that would be necessary would be to have the points standardized and the holes drilled in the proper place so that the farmer might be able to go to any plough firm and get the necessary repairs for his machine. The same thing applies to plough sole plates. Let us take blower pipes, which are very much in use. Farmers throughout the country are erecting silos and it is necessary to procure a lot of .piping. These pipes could with very little expense be standardized and it would be a great blessing to any farmer using a silo filler. Next we have the question of wagon arms. Now, I would not say that the arm should be standardized, but I contend that the nuts should have the same thread on all wagons. It would cost practically nothing to change the present nuts so as have the threads on all arms of wagons the same. If that were done a farmer who lost a nut off his wagon would not have to go to five or six different repair houses to get his wagon fixed up. Thei'e are some other articles on the list such as machine bolts, etc., and while I do not refer to them, I think I have said enough to show the inconvenience to which users of agricultural implements have been put in securing parts for their machines. This is why I am anxious to have this matter brought to the attention of the House. Now, some manufacturers might tell hon. members that they are keeping a large supply of repairs for their particular line of goods in every agency and municipality throughout the country. Well, why did the provincial legislature of Saskatchewan pass the legislation that it did during last session? I quote the following from "Canadian Farm Implements:"
The Saskatchewan Farm Implement Act has been altered by the addition of two new pro-
visions. The first provides a penalty of $100 for each offence where a vendor fails to maintain a sufficient supply of repairs required for machines sold by him and in operation in the province; and the second authorize the Minister of Agriculture to appoint inspectors whose duties shall be to inspect the stocks of repairs kept by vendors and who shall have free access during business hours to the vendors' premises.
This goes to show the importance of having a repair stock kept on hand by different vendors in the agricultural implement business. It is evident that a lot of agencies have not been keeping repairs to supply the farmers; otherwise, it would not have been necessary for the provincial legislature to pass this legislation. If the repair parts were standardized as I suggest it would be unnecessary for a lot of different agents to keep a full stock because one stock would supply the demand in small towns and villages throughout the country. As hon. members know, there are many articles in common household use now that are standardized. It was not such a long time ago when we could not get an electric bulb that would fit any socket. To-day all bulbs are standardized and the convenience in consequence is incalculable. The same thing applies to plumbing; we have plumbing repairs standardized so as to be interchangeable. And so far as automobiles are concerned, tires and rims are standardized; so that a man, regardless of the kind of car he owns, can easily get these parts of his, car from any dealer. Now, we have a precedent for standardization of farming implements in action that has been taken abroad, and I might read from "Canadian Farm Implements," printed in Winnipeg, the following:
The Standard Committee of the American Society of Agricultural Engineers reports that excellent progress has been made in stadard-ization during 1920. The following standards are now ready for final adoption. Standard belt speeds, in which it is proposed to include five speeds, viz., 1,500, 2,600, 3,000, 3,250 and 3,500 feet per minute. Standard tractor and plough hitches, which include height of vertical hitch on tractor and lateral adjustments for ploughs of two, three and four bottoms.
Farm wagon standards, including the standard automobile track of 56 inches and tire widths for wuigons of various capacity ratings.
The following standards are in the process of development:
A standard code for testing and rating the belt and drawbar power of tractors.
A standard manger form for dairy barns.
Standard ratings for letter carrier capacities and dimensions.
Standard ratings for capacities and power requirements of ensilage cutters.
This is not an entirely new matter. It started in the United States in many

different lines and I feel satisfied that if we do not carry out legislation in the same direction we shall be very much behind the times. I think that the benefits to be derived from the standardization of parts of agricultural machinery are so obvious that this matter needs no great argument. This question has been directed to the attention of many prominent men in this country who are interested in agriculture, as, for instance, the Minister of Agriculture in the government of Ontario, the Hon. Mr. Doherty. I desire in this connection to quote the following:
I represent the United Farmers of Ontario. This matter has been up for discussion at meetings of the United Farmers during the past year It is a very live question with the farmers of the province. They are very quick to see the immense advantages that would accrue to them from the standardization of the wearable and breakable parts of their machines. Last fall there was a meeting of the Fairs and Exhibitions Association in Toronto, and they discussed this matter at some considerable length, and passed a resolution. I only refer to these matters to show the members of this Committee that the farmers of the province of Ontario will appreciate anything you can accomplish along the line which you are now following, and would he very grateful for any results that can be secured, along that line. I congratulate you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee upon taking up a question that is of such vital importance to the farmers. At the Fairs and Exhibitions Association, in which 350 agricultural societies of Ontario are represented, the following resolution was passed:
"That this Association in Convention assembled hereby express their hearty approval of the standardization of the breakable and wearable parts of farm machinery and would respectfully recommend that the Federal Government arrange for a committee of mechanical experts, three to be appointed by the Federal Government and three by the manufacturers of farming implements to arrange for such standardization and that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to Sir Robert Borden and Hon. T. A. Crerar."
This statement, Mr. Speaker, only goes to show that the farmers of this country know how important this question is. They know the hardships everybody engaged in farming has to contend with during the busy harvesting time and they know how easy it would be for the manufacturers of our country to standardize some of the parts I have referred to. I hope the members of the House will give this matter their most serious consideration and will follow it up by according their support to the resolution. I feel satisfied that if they do so, the users of agricultural implements will be extremely grateful to this Parliament. The Canadian manufacturers of agricultural implements will not be hurt to any extent but will be fortunate in the years to come
to be in the happy position that they will be able to secure in European markets, as well as at home, the patronage of the users of agricultural implements for their machinery, in preference to the implements of foreign manufacturers.

maintopic: STANDARDIZATION OF PARTS OF AGRICULTURAL MACHINERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact, as the mover of the resolution has remarked, that this question is not a new one but has received some consideration from the House in previous sessions, I, as chairman of the Select Standing Committee on Agriculture, before whom a full discussion of the matter took place and upon whose advice arrangements have been made for the carrying on of an investigation with regard to securing all the necessary information as to what would be a proper solution of this very important question, deem it to be my privilege and my duty, to make a few observations at this time. I wish it distinctly understood that any remarks I have to make will be perfectly in accord with those of the last speaker as to the desirability of a standardization of the important parts of agricultural implements. But my special object in speaking on the present occasion, is to draw attention to the fact that the Standing Committee on Agriculture has been giving consideration to this question for a considerable time, and that it has appointed a sub-committee to conduct an investigation and to hold conferences with manufacturers who are directly interested in the other side of the question. I may state that such conferences have been held and such discussions carried on, as tend to throw some light on this important question. Further, the matter is still under review by the Committee on Agriculture. The first meeting of that committee for the present session, which is now arranged for, has on its agenda the taking up of business left over from the sittings Of the committee last session. Under that heading the present question will come under review. No doubt the sub-committee, of which the mover of the resolution is a member, will make certain recommendations to the general committee. Then the Standing Committee on Agriculture, with all the facts before it, will bring in certain recommendations to the House. Therefore in view of what has been done by that committee, and the sub-committee as well, I think it would be better for the House to defer any lengthened discussion of the matter until such time as the findings of the committee are brought down. I therefore beg to

move in amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Harold):
That all the words after the word "that" in the first paragraph of the said resolution be struck out and that the whole question incorporated in the Motion before the House be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Agriculture for their further consideration, requesting said Committee to bring in such recommendations as their investigation of the facts will warrant.
