subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION

speakeroldname: Mr. F. H. KEEFER (Port Arthur and Kenora) moved:
subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, a Special Committee consisting of	members should
be appointed to consider and investigate the benefits to be derived from a deep waterway for transportation from the Great Lakes to the sea by way of the St. Lawrence river, having regard in particular to the benefits arising from the then increased navigation facilities and the utilization of the Hydro-Electric energy of the St. Lawrence river, and that the Special Committee have power to hold sessions in Ottawa or elsewhere during the recess of Parliament and have power to call for persons, papers, or records and to examine witnesses, under oath, and to report from time to time to this House.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the deepening of the St. Lawrence river has been pronounced by some of the best minds of the United States and Canada as probably one of the greatest economic questions of the day. It is greatest in its magnitude, greatest in the benefits which its accomplishment would bring about. It is desirable, therefore, that the matter should be investigated by members of the House so that when we return to our constituencies we can, in turn, explain it to them, and it is with that purpose in view that I have
 moved this resolution. I hope that the press will do all that they can to give publicity to the matter.
I think it advisable to give at this stage a short account of the history of the deep waterway transportation question from the Great Lakes to the sea, by way of the St. Lawrence river. About two years ago five of the states of the Northwest United States organized themselves into a body known as the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Tidewater Association, with the sole object of endeavouring to get their products to the sea. To show you how serious they were in the matter, I may point out that each of these states subscribed $10,000 from their legislative moneys, making a fund of $50,000 to carry on a propaganda at Washington. They went to Washington with their senators and congressmen, and, of course, the Administration granted their request, and the matter was referred to the International Joint Commission. The International Joint Commission then received from the two Governments certain questions to be answered-questions of a twofold nature, one economic, and the other engineering. Each Government appointed an engineer to assist the Commission and prepare estimates as to what the cost of the project would be. The Commission has been holding sessions all over Canada and the United States; with, I believe, one more sitting at Detroit they will conclude their public hearings, and it is expected that their report will be published in Ottawa about the second week in April, when their regular statutory sittings are held.
Now, this motion for a committee is in no way to interfere with or to derogate from the International Joint Commission. It is important that we come to understand this question just as our cousins to the South have understood it. They have realized the importance of it; it is equally important to us-not, of course, in point of population, the United States outnumbering us ten to one, but the benefit is common in all other respects.
I should like to say a few words with regard to the benefits that will be derived from this project when completed. They are two-fold in their nature, one affecting the question of transportation, and the other the question of fuel and the development of power as a substitute for fuel. As regards transportation, it goes without saying that it is the tie which binds the different parts of the country together. If isolated parts of a dominion or an empire are without means of transportation, with-

out means of getting to or from the centres or the markets, the sentiment of attachment slowly dies out, and, feeling their isolation, the separated parts are liable to drop off and fall away. It is apparent therefore, that the development of means of transportation is bound to 9 p.m,. promote the public good. I would like our friends in the prairie country to realize that the problem in no way conflicts with that which is very dear to their hearts-the Hudson Bay Railway project. When the International Joint Commission held sittings at various points on the prairies the suggestion was made that there might be an interference in this connection. But we do not wish in any way to interfere with the Hudson Bay Railway project; this proposal in no way touches it or affects it.
Now, what are the benefits of these transportation facilities? I have lived for some thirty years at the head of the Lakes. Originally the movement of freight was from the East to the West. I have seen the wheat going into the West steadily and none going out, and I have seen, as is the condition to-day, hundreds of millions of bushels going from the West to the East. Heretofore Canada has endeavoured to meet this situation by the use of her canal systems but owing to the changes which have taken place we are now behind the times. We ship the grain from Port Arthur in vessels carrying 500,000 bushels, but vessels of that kind can only go as far as Port Colborne, and it takes four ships of present Welland and St. Lawrence canal size to carry that same cargo from Port Colborne to Montreal. Necessarily, because of the large carrying capacity, the freight charge to Port Colborne or to Buffalo is lower than it is for the comparatively short distance from Port Colborne to Montreal. The rate last year was four cents from the head of the Lakes to Port Colborne or Buffalo, a voyage occupying about five days. If the rate for that five days trip is four cents a bushel, it is not unreasonable to assume that for two days additional journey the rate would be an additional two cents a bushel. If therefore, the vessel did not have to discharge at Port Colborne, the rate through to Montreal from Port Arthur, Duluth or Chicago would be six cents a bushel. But under the present procedure the grain does not go to Montreal; it is unloaded at Buffalo and shipped to New York. It costs twelve cents a bushel to get it from Buffalo to New York by rail and the barge canal rate is now prac-43i
tically the same as the rail rate. People do not realize that Buffalo or Port Colborne are as near to the market at, say, Liverpool by the St. Lawrence as New York is in distance.
That being the case, why unnecessarily transport this grain four or five hundred miles more to New York and have that cost of transporting the grain and then be just as far away as when you were at Buffalo? I make the statement that there will be to every producer of grain in the West a direct saving the moment a ship can go straight through with a large cargo to Montreal, instead of breaking bulk en route. When the vessel is at Montreal, she is three or four hundred miles nearer Liverpool than if she were at New York, and the rate from Montreal to Liverpool is the same as the rate from New York to Liverpool. It is quite clear that you can save five cents a bushel on all the grains of the West if they can be moved without breaking bulk at the foot of lake Erie. Let me explain the reason why. The price of every article is, of course, governed by the market, and the market for our grain is in Europe. The producer, the farmer in the West, gets that market price, less the cost, including brokerage, insurance and everything else, of getting his product to the market. If, therefore, you can reduce the transportation charges by five cents, you are going to put that saving into every producer's pocket, and it needs no mathematical computation by me to show how the producers of the West are going to benefit. Grain for export and grain which is used for home consumption command the same price. So much for grain.
As regards flour, the moment you handle any package freight, the cost runs up very largely, and the saving on package freight will be very large. One of the problems with which this country has to grapple is to get the flour out instead of simply moving out the grain, because it is very much more profitable to Canada to ship out flour and to keep the by-products of grain in our country as far as we can than it is to ship out wheat. One can readily see that on articles like dairy produce, canned goods and package freight of that kind, that has to be handled two or three times, the saving will be considerable. I should like to call the attention of hon. members to what I found in my mail box this morning. This is a newspaper called the Weekly Market News and Financial Farmer. I do not

know where or by whom it is published. It was sent to me as a marked copy containing a report of the Wheat Board; but in it is a copy of an address given by Julius H. Barnes, who was formerly Wheat Director and President of the United States Grain Corporation, and with the permission of the House I should like to read what Mr. Barnes said in his address to the Farmers Marketing Committee of Seventeen at Chicago on November 5, 1920. Mr. Barnes Is the recognized authority in the United States on these questions. In the middle of his address he speaks of the improvement possible in the relative position of the producer, and under the head of water transportation he says:
It follows then that a project such as that before the country to-day of so improving the "St. Lawrence that ocean carriers reach the western ports of the Great Lakes or that the' Lake *carriers may deliver their cargoes alongside the ocean carriers in the St. Lawrence instead of breaking the hulk at Buffalo, deserves the earnest consideration and support of those who have at heart the improvement of the relative position of the western producer.
Then he goes on to say:
Its relation to the farm delivery cost simply stated is this:	The present rail rate from
Buffalo to New York is twelve cents per bushel. Also, to reach Montreal, the rail rate from Georgian bay is also approximately 12 cents per bushel. Ocean carriers may be secured at the same rate from Montreal as from New York. The opening of the St. Lawrence waterway and the improvement of the Welland canal, already undertaken by Canada, would enable the lake carrier to Buffalo to extend its trip to Montreal-only forty-eight hours longer-at a cost probably not exceeding two cents per bushel. This promises a saving of ten cents a bushel during part of the year. Its influence may reasonably be calculated to affect and improve the farm price by five cents per bushel on the entire grain crops of. that section of the country whose arc of competitive rail rates would thus be centred on the Great lakes ports -Duluth, Chicago, Milwaukee, Detroit, Toledo, Cleveland.
He is speaking from the point of view of the United States side of the line and, of course, what he says is equally applicable to the Canadian side.
This applies to home consumption as well as *exportable surplus, so it may reasonably be calculated on some 4,000,000,000 bushels of grain *or $200,000,000 annually.
If the United States and Canada could realize that they are losing to the producers of grain $200,000,000 annually by not setting this canal built, I think we would get a little more rapid movement than we have had so far. There are in the United States some gentlemen who, since this organization started, made this statement -and I believe it can be justified when you compute the package freight as well

as everything else-that it would pay the two countries, Canada and the United States, to build this canal each year anu tear it down and rebuild it rather than, continue without it as at present. If that be true, or anywhere nearly true, the question arises, even if we are hard up, even if we need to conserve in every respect, which is better-to spend some money on this project and pay sinking fund and interest upon it and have something from year to year, or to throw away twice, or three times, or five times the amount annually? , That is what the situation is going to boil down to. I feel perfectly certain that when the Government and this House realize the financial side of this question, they will not allow this project to be delayed any longer. So much for the question of package freight.
I see the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) opposite me. I hope to see the day when a ship will be able to come with coal from his town of Sydney up to the head of the lakes and deliver it there, which is a thing that cannot be done to-day. Ontario is and has been suffering from a coal famine, and I cannot see why that coal should not be marketed in Ontario and brought up even to the head of the lakes and used on the railways further west. Every year large. quantities of Pennsylvania coal are brought up to the head of the lakes and stored for railway systems. There is, to my mind, no reason why, if those vessels did not have to break bulk, they could not load with coal in Nova Scotia, carry it right to the head of the lakes and bring back grain which could be shipped overseas from Nova Scotia.
Somebody may say, as has frequently been said, that this will never be used by salt water ships, but it is rather difficult to say these days that anything will not happen. Let us think for a moment what is happening. The Kiel canal did not simply open up a new navigation system; it shortened a journey by about three or four hundred miles. Formerly, ships could go round by Jutland; now they go through the Kiel canal, thus saving three or four hundred miles, and before the war many ships were using that route. We know the situation in regard to the Suez canal. What is the effect of the Panama canal, which is a locking system and which is quite a long one?
Let me show you what effect the Panama Canal has had upon the Middle States and

the same thing will apply to our Middle , Northwest. In Montana the Anaconda mine produces zinc and copper ores. The market for that zinc and copper is New York city. To transport it by rail would cost so much. Since the Panama Canal has been built, the owners of that mine have found that by shipping their product to Seattle, and then by vessels through the Panama Canal to New York, they are saving six cents a hundred pounds in freights, or $1,000,000 a year. They transport by rail to Seattle, on the Pacific coast, I said, which is exactly the same distance from their mine as Duluth, upon Lake Superior. They could transport their product to Duluth by rail, and the rate ought to be less because they do not have to climb the divide. Then from Duluth to New York by water, the rate is forty per cent, of what it is from Seattle, and therefore it is computed they will save at least three cents a pound, which will amount to a saving of $500,000 per annum on that one mine, if they could ship without breaking bulk from Duluth by water. So h: will "be with many another industry in Canada and the United States.
Ah, but some say, you will never have coastwise trade from the Great Lakes to the sea board. Why not? If the Strait of Gibraltar were not open boats would nci; go past there, but as it is open, the boats do go in. It is much longer to go around by Gibraltar from the Baltic ports than to ship across land by rail, and yet the produce of all those countries goes round by water. The route to Constantinople is 800 or 900 miles longer by water than by rail, yet the freight from, say, Antwerp or London, all goes by water. Why should not the same thing happen here? Why should not ships from Boston, New York and inland ports on the great lake system use this waterway once it is open?
Take another example of a canal. Manchester was feeling the loss of her manufacturing business. In order to get rid of the high cost of handling, manufacturing firms were moving away from Manchester to the sea board. A man, I think, by the name of Stevenson hammered away until he got the Manchester Ship Canal built. It is some 35 miles long, with 5 locks. What has been the result of the building of that canal? To-day Manchester is the third largest shipping port in Great Britain. Now, if salt water ships will go up that 35 miles of canal and through 5 locks, for the traffic coming out of the one port of Manchester, why should not salt water ships come up this inland waterway to Buffalo, Detroit, Erie, Chicago and Ontario
ports, and serve both them and the whole country tributary thereto? Why, Mr. Speaker, there is no country in the world that is so rich in products natural and manufactured as the Great Lakes country. You take any area 300 or 400 miles away from the Great Lakes and draw a line round on the map and see what you cover. Look at the natural timber wealth, look at the natural mineral wealth, look at the agricultural wealth and the manufacturing wealth of all those cities and prairie towns. This waterway would double and treble the transportation facilities, and the nlinute you reduced the cost of freights you would get articles moving that are not moving now.
Some may say that salt water ships would not be able to come up on account of their draught. They may not want to come, but they do elsewhere. Salt water ships go a thousand miles up the Amazon river. Now, ships can float in fresh water as in salt, and on the question of draught, let me give you some figures of the large ports of the world. The depth at Odessa, the great wheat port of Russia, is only 24 feet, Petrograd, 19 1-2 feet, Riga 23 feet, Libau 271-2 feet, Constantinople 22 feet. Our canals are going down to 30 feet on the sill, and 25 feet in the channel of over 800 feet in length and when the Welland Canal and the St. Lawrence canals are built, it is estimated that 86 per cent, of the salt water tonnage can, if it wishes, reach Lake Erie. The popular idea is that ships are too large to come up these canals, but the number of very large ships on the ocean is very small compared with the number of tramp vessels, just as the number of Pullman cars is relatively small compared with the number of box cars on the railways. The number of vessels that draw more than 24 feet of water is relatively small. You have a few Mauretanias, Lusitanias, Leviathans, and so forth, but not many, while you have thousands of tramp vessels carrying only freight cargoes. I expect to see the day when these ships can find their way into any port on this inland Mediterranean. In the early days I have as a lawyer protested a ship from Antwerp, coming up the lakes with a cargo of rails. Now if that ship can come over from Antwerp, I cannot see why, if the canal is made large enough, any other salt water ship cannot come. These vessels will not take the place of our fresh water marine. These vessels are built for quick transportation with 30 or 40 hatches than can be quickly opened and shut, ensuring rapid

receiving and rapid delivery. They will always continue to handle iron ore and wheat. A tramp steamer may occasionally come in for a cargo of wheat, but these tramp vessels in the main would take a large amount of stuff that is not now moving, but that would move if the freight rate was reduced. They would take dairy products, for instance, and any kind of package freight, and it is in that kind of freight that the cost of handling runs up very fast on account of there being so much handling in and out of cars, vessels, and freight sheds. That class of business would materially be benefited. Meats, bacon, and all that sort of thing would move more freely and cheaply. One of the chief objections to this route has come from the city of Buffalo. It was very pleasant indeed to be in Montreal, and to observe the contrast. Each of these two places was largely affected in the same manner. They feared the stoppage of breaking in bulk. Montreal took the broad view and said that what was good for Canada was good for Montreal. Buffalo said: Why, this will ruin Buffalo. You take a 10,000 ton ship that comes to Buffalo and it means employment for so many hands to get the freight out of the ship, transport it across to the railway car, and get it to New York; the same thing in New York, and vice versa on the return. " Exactly," said those opponents of Buffalo in the West. " That is what we want to stop. We do not want to continue paying that tribute to you unnecessarily, and that will be the effect. Buffalo will however gain greatly by this development; she will become a seaport as near to Liverpool as New York is. She will have the Erie Canal to bring in by barge freight a large amount of manufactured products from the centres of industrial life, and instead of losing business she will gain." On the contrary, it is pleasing to see that Montreal took the view that even though she should lose she would not stand in the way of the development of the great West of Canada.
The other phase of the question is that of Hydro-Electric energy. It has been estimated that on the St. Lawrence river the horsepower available is some 4,000,000 and only a small fraction thereof has been used. It could not all be used at once, nor could it be consumed for some time to come. But we are rapidly running short of electrical energy. We of Ontario know what the significance has been during the last two years of orders coming from the HydroElectric : " shut off your current for such
IMr. Keefer.]
and such a time." It is a serious thing for the industrial life of the country. What would be the effect of this in a town thar depended on this electric energy? Ordinarily it is estimated, I think, that it takes ten tons of coal for one horsepower. That means $100 per horsepower, 'and yet we can do it Hydro-Electrically for $25. Why do we not do it? Simply because we are asleep. We are wasting that much money all the time. Ontario has awakened to this fact until she has used up all the power produced at Niagara Falls and is building a canal down to Queenstown, the intention being practically to scrap the plants built at Niagara Falls eventually in order to get the full benefit or head of the water there. We have 4,000,000 horsepower Tuning to waste on the St. Lawrence. Practically three-fourths of that is Canadian. That 4,000,000 horsepower would represent 40,000,000 tons of coal. We are importing every year fifteen or twenty million tons of coal, going on our knees to the United States to obtain it, and paying high exr change for it. The day is not very far distant when that coal will not be allowed to come into this country, for eventually it will have to be conserved for use in the United States. It behooves us, therefore, seriously to consider this matter. I see that the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) has a motion on the Order Paper asking for a committee to investigate the coal question, and I think it would be well for him to associate himself with this motion and, if we get that committee, to bring out before it the facts which he desires to deal with. Once the barrier at the St. Lawrence is open we can have coal come up from Nova Scotia or anywhere else, even Swansea, England, or any other place. Coal carriers do come over from the Old Country to United States ports and I see no reason why they could not enter Canadian ports as well. If we once get this energy developed there will be between Montreal and Toronto on both sides of the river the greatest hive of industrial life that the world has ever seen. We do not realize what it means. If we can once get the people to realize that there is any quantity of electrical energy there that can be developed steadily, with industry after industry located there, it will mean an enormous benefit for Canada, because they can get their power cheap as well as transportation to and from there on the highway of the sea. The salt water ships can come to them, and the point is an ideal manufacturing one.

I do not know that there is anything in regard to which the whole of Canada would he so greatly benefited. I have roughly outlined the benefit that would accrue to the farming community of the West, and the consumer would be benefited by the increased production that would ensue. Why should Boston and the large cities of the East be short of food when it is rotting in the interior? The cry all the time is "No cars." In addition to that, the cost of manufactured articles should be reduced because of the cheapness of electricity. I hope, therefore, that this House will begin to study this question and try to realize that although we are hard up and need to be careful and not spend money unnecessarily, we should not continue to lose money as we are doing at the present time.
That is the whole gist of the motion. I do not know a better time at which this matter could be brought up. This project would be mutually beneficial to the two countries. The United States and Canada would be co-operating in its construction and that could have only one result, namely, a great benefit. It would also be worldwide in its effects in the cheapening of products. And above all things, I do not think there is a. better time for us to begin to tackle this question. It will take a year yet before we can get the proper engineering data to tackle the question. But, Mr. Speaker, let us look at this matter in the light of a peace memorial. Just before the war broke out in 1914 there was under way a project to construct an international bridge at Niagara as a memorial to the hundred years of peace between Great Britain and the United States, and it does seem to me that a work like this, international in character, would make one of the finest peace memorials and of our cooperation as allies which we could possibly conceive.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) and I find that his resolution calls for a special committee consisting of an unspecified number of members for the consideration and investigation of the benefits to be derived from a deep waterway for transportation from the Great Lakes to the sea by way of the St. Lawrence river. The House is very well aware of the fact that a similar commission was appointed some years ago to study the water-powers, the water levels, and the whole question which my hon.
friend would like to have investigated at the present time, and that that commission decided at the time, after a study of the St. Lawrence waterway, that the only possible settlement of the transportation question by way of water would be from the Great Lakes down through the Ottawa river to Montreal.
There were very many reasons adduced in favour of the project, some of which my hon. friend (Mr. Keefer) has mentioned this evening. I recall the discussion of this matter in this House upon different occasions. I remember it was pointed out that our Nova Scotia coal could not get farther west than Montreal owing to the expense of its carriage by rail; but that by the construction of the Georgian Bay Canal, Nova Scotia, coal could be transported up the Ottawa river. The great advantage of the Ottawa River route over the St. Lawrence route, which my hon. friend endorses to-night, is that it would give the whole of the upper Ottawa country, and all the lands within reach of the Ottawa river, a chance of being developed. There are untold natural resources in that country, but they cannot be developed and the products carried out at present because of the expensive rail rates. Still there are a considerable number who were not in Parliament when the discussion of the Georgian Bay Canal project invariably formed part' of the proceedings of the House on one, if not two days of each session. Mr. Speaker, as one of the
members of the House who live upon the Great Lakes, I should like to say a few words upon this question. In speaking to the subject dealt with by the member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) I do not wish it to be thought by anybody that this is a proposal put forward by the head of the Lakes, including Port Arthur and Fort William. As a matter of fact the proposal, as my hon. friend pointed out, was originally put forward within the last year or two by committees on the American side, in conjunction with committees on the Canadian side, particularly committees from the neigbourhood of the constituency of my hon. friend from North Essex (Mr. Kennedy). It was at a meeting of that committee that this idea developed for the working out of some scheme whereby ocean freighters could enter the Great Lakes and make of the Great Lakes an American Mediterranean. Any one, Sir, who has read the fascinating stories of Parkman with regard to the original explorations about the shores of the Great Lakes must naturally be interested in such a question as this. When we remember that it was the men, those old French voyageurs particularly, who explored every mile of the Great Lakes, and down to the mouth of the Mississippi,-men like La Salle, Marquette, Joliet, Duluth, De la Verendrye, and those other great explorers who went from the mouth of the St. Lawrence and up through the Lakes, through what is proposed as the Georgian Bay route by my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) and also through what is proposed as the southern route by the committee that has been discussing this question-when we

remember that, the matter is one of romantic interest to all of us.
With regard to the Georgian Bay Canal,
I may point out to my hon. friend from Wright, who, naturally, by virtue of the fact that his constituency would be more interested in the building of that canal than in the carrying out of the southern route project, is a supporter of that scheme .-that the parts of the Great Lakes west of the Sault are as much interested in the Georgian Bay canal as they would be in the carrying out of the southern or St. Lawrence route project. So far as Port Arthur and Fort William are concerned we would be just as much pleased up there to see the Georgian Bay route built as the southern route. But since the Government of Canada has undertaken to spend some seventy or eighty million of dollars upon the Welland canal, and since the great industrial part of Canada so far as Ontario is concerned is situated along the southern route, it appears that the most
10 p.m. likely proposal to be gone on with is the southern route, and it appears also that that southern route would obtain a great deal more traffic than the northern route. The question of the building of the Georgian Bay canal has been discussed at the head of the lakes as far back as I can remember, and the construction of that route would be received with as great pleasure as the other. But the point is that opportunities come, perhaps, in one particular direction and we are ready for them as they come. So that with regard to this question I am supporting in a general way the project for the building of one of these canals.
A point for my hon. friends in Quebec to remember is that Montreal is closer by about five hundred miles to London and Liverpool than New York is. That can hardly be believed until one looks at the map and observes the exact directions of traffic. Another point which is worth remembering is that the area of the Great Lakes and the industrial part of Ontario are not, the only parts of the country interested in this project. It is stated by the American supporters of this scheme-and there are many more of them than there are Canadian supporters of it-that one-third of the population and one-third of the area of the United States are concerned in matters affecting the states bordering on the Great Lakes; and they go on to say that seventy per cent of the raw materials and foods produced in the United States are
produced in the neighbourhood of the Great Lakes. That naturally makes the southern route of much more importance from the commercial standpoint than the Georgian Bay route. In the Georgian Bay route the ships would have to go up around Lake Nip-issing, up around the Georgian bay, down lake Huron, and then make a circuitous trip in order to tap such parts of the Great Lakes as those around lake Ontario and lake Erie. It is worth while pointing out the amount of traffic which is going through the Soo canal much of which would be influenced or affected by the building of a southern route. In 1855, 106,000 tons passed through the Soo canal; in 1881,
2.000.	000 tons; in 1891, 8,000,000; in 1901,
24.000.	000 tons; in 1916, 70,000,000 tons. It is said that the amount of tonnage passing through the Soo canal is four times the amount which passes through the Suez canal.
Some hon. gentleman-either the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) or the member for Wright-remarks that ships have in the past taken advantage of this route to go up the Great Lakes. I well remember when I was a boy-and that was quite a few years ago now-seeing a Norwegian vessel which had travelled across the Atlantic ocean and which came through the Welland canal and unloaded a cargo at Fort William. True, it was a small vessel, but this goes to show that vessels have already made this trip. It is a fact also that during the war a number of small war vessels were built for the French Government at the head of the lakes.. Therefore, this fioute has already been navigated to a certain extent.
It is true that before the war $100,000,000 or $200,000,000 was looked upon as a vast amount of money to think of spending on transportation routes, such as railways or canals, or any other investment of that kind, but since Canada alone has spent in the war something like $2,000,000,000, perhaps a question of this kind will receive more kindly consideration and will not be looked upon with so much dread because of the fact that it might cost Canada $100,000,000 or $200,000,000. The fact that there are, as my hon. friend (Mr. Keefer) has pointed out, some
4,000,000 horsepower of potential electrical energy in the waterfalls of the St. Lawrence river must be considered. We can get some idea of what that means when we realize that in Canada there is said to be some 18,000,000 or 20,000,000 horsepower of potential electrical energy

of which only 2,000,000 horsepower has so far been developed.
My hon. friend also pointed out that there would be a saving in the cost of transportation of wheat. That means that on every bushel of wheat grown in the West which is exported-and that includes about 80 per cent of the wheat of the West-there would be a possible saving of from five to ten cents. My hon. friend read part of a speech delivered by Mr. Julius ^Barnes who is known to every hon. member who has had any dealings with the wheat question, and in that address Mr. Barnes pointed out that there might be a saving of ten cents a bushel. In other words, it would probably cost ten cents a bushel less to take wheat from Buffalo to Montreal than from Buffalo to New York. It might be worth while recalling that in the past 65 per cent of the wheat of the Canadian West has gone by Buffalo to New York, so that this canal would be the means of bringing that Canadian traffic back to Canadian channels again.
Whatever opposition has come to this proposition has come from New York and Buffalo, and without blaming them in any way for the stand they are taking, one must admit that their stand is taken from an entirely selfish point of view, just as I presume our standpoint may be regarded as a selfish one from the outlook of those Canadians who live on the shores of the Great lakes. But at the same time this is a matter which is of the utmost moment to those living not only on the shores of the Great lakes, but on the vast prairies of the West, not only of Canada, but of the United States. It has been stated by authorities that 80 per cent of the present ocean freighters could utilize these canals once they were built without these canals being made to a depth greater thafn 24 feet. In other words that means that only 20 per cent of the ocean freighters are so large that they could not use this route.
In closing these rather desultory remarks, I should like to point out the importance of the international aspect of this question. We cannot help remembering that for over 100 years the United States and Canada have been living side by side without a fort on either side of the international boundary line, without a gun pointing across the boundary, and this would be of the utmost importance as an example to the rest of the world how two great countries, the United 
States and Canada, can join together to build up such an important international project as this.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) this evening, and I think the members of this House are indebted to that hon. gentleman for the very clear and lucid exposition of facts that he gave us in connection with this project. To-day, there are agitating the minds of most of the thinking people of this country two great questions that are very closely allied, one being the question of transportation of all kinds and the other the question of freight rates. The recent increase that was granted in freight rates was granted, *so I understood and so it was stated in the press, in order that the railway companies might operate without from month to month, having a deficit which they were threatened with on account of increased cost of oneration. So far as I have been able to judge from the financial statements that have been published, I am not quite sure that the rail- way companies have benefited by the increases; but I know the increased freight rates have succeeded in stifling manufacture, in limiting production and in increasing the cost of the necesaries of life in every home in this land. Therefore, it seems to me that any project that has for its purpose the lowering of freight rates is one that should meet with the approval of the people generally, and the motion of the hon. gentleman this evening asking for consideration of this project by a special committee, is one that should be readily granted by this House.
The war has changed to a certain extent the alignment of trade. We in Canada hope to make this a great exporting nation, not only' of natural, but of manufactured products, and if we are to take our products abroad, if we are to meet competition in the open markets of the world, surely one thing that we need more than almost anything else is all the assistance we can have in the way of low carrying charges. There are two elements that enter into the matter-the carrying of the raw material and the carrying of the finished products. Low freight rates will not only enable us to meet competition abroad, but mean that we shall be gainers as regards our domestic business. As has been said in this House this evening by one hon. gentleman in speaking of the probable cost of this project, it will

mean a large expenditure of public money.
I am not insensible of the financial condition of this country to-day. I appreciate that this is a country with a population of approximately 9,000,000 people; that we have a net debt of over $2,300,000,000 and that it is asking everything that the people of this country can bear to meet the fixed charges upon that debt. I appreciate too that there is throughout this country to-day a demand on the part of the people that there shall be retrenchment in regard to the actual expense of carrying on government, and also that there shall be a cessation of borrowings in connection with capital charges. But there are capital charges and capital charges. It is one thing to incur an expenditure in connection with a massive pile of buildings that do not earn one dollar of income during the year, and that probably cause an increased expenditure in the way of maintenance and other charges in connection therewith, while it is quite another thing to spend money in developing a project such as that pointed out by the hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer), one that will mean lower freight rates, cheaper carrying charges and, in addition to that, the development of electrical energy that, if the figures quoted to-night are correct, will mean that interest charges on the capital expended will be met from that source.
Those of us who live in municipalities that border on the Great Lakes or on their tributaries are keenly interested in this project. In the city of Windsor two years ago we had a meeting of the International Waterways Commission, and when the people of that city had the facts presented to them and an opportunity of considering the question as it was discussed at that convention, they were unanimous in their approval of thi^ project. I believe that would apply equally well to the people throughout the Dominion; and if this Government will grant the committee that is asked for, so that the facts will be adduced, and considering, I believe, it will have the approval of the people in connection with such an outlay.
I rise also to-night for the reason that, with your permission, Sir, I desire to place on Hansard a telegram that I have received from the chairman of the Board of Commerce of our city. This telegram reads:
The Border Chamber of Commerce unanimously and emphatically endorsed deepening of the St. Lawrence waterways and the development of the power consequent thereon, as advocated by Canadian Deep Waterways and Power Association organized at Windsor in November, 1919. We believe this to be greatest economic project of the age.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, lest any one should come to the conclusion that only those living at the head of the lakes or in the country immediately bordering on the lakes are interested in this particular question,
I rise simply as one from the far West to give endorsement to the proposal introduced by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer). I may say that I certainly was not a supporter of this project until recently, not that I knew anything particular about it, but as my hon. friend from Port Arthur has said, a very large number of our people have been opposed to this project simply because they believed it would kill the Hudson Bay railway. Let me say as emphatically as I can that if I thought for one minute that this canal system was going to kill the Hudson Bay Railway project, or injure it in any way,
I for one would not support this proposal, because for years, like thousands of others in Western Canada, I have been thoroughly convinced of the feasibility and practicability of the Hudson Bay route, and I am thoroughly satisfied that as soon as this Government can find the money to complete that project, and does so, it will be a success. But I have been led by the hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) to look into this deep waterway scheme in the past year or two, because I have always found them men who took a keen interest in practical questions as opposed to academic or theoretical questions. A project that was practical always found their support, and they are the kind of men I like to associate myself with. So I looked into this scheme, and I have come to the conclusion that it has very substantial merit, and that the Canadian people ought to give it their very best attention.
What has surprised me most is the ease with which the scheme can be carried out? Had I been asked some time ago whether or not it was a difficult engineering problem, I think I would have answered, as thousands of other Canadians would, that it was too difficult altogether for the Canadian people to undertake, but when I find that there are only some 40 miles of canalization necessary, and that those who have investigated the project estimate that it would require only about $100,000,000, and that there is a drop only of some 220 feet, I say at once that it is not such a

tremendous project that the Canadian people need be afraid of it. Why, even the Welland canal comes almost up to it in magnitude. The Welland canal, I understand, is 25 miles long and has a drop of over 300 feet, so the project at present under discussion is not much greater than what we have already done. Such being the case, why need we be afraid of it? My own opinion is that if the St. Lawrence waterway had been wholly within the Dominion of Canada or wholly within the United States this project would long since have been carried to completion, but the difficulty is that it is an international waterway, and as a consequence a great deal of unnecessary delay has occurred.
Now, why should we support this scheme? My candid opinion is that it will be of such enormous benefit to the whole of Canada, and particularly Western Canada, in increasing production that we cannot afford to do without it. My hon. friend from Port Arthur has suggested to-night that if we had this deep waterway scheme we would save 5 cents a bushel on every bushel of wheat we produced. We would make that much, if his figures are correct, for that is what it amounts to. In a case such as this, it is not the consumer who pays, because we must deliver our grain from Canada to Liverpool in competition with the grain with the rest of the world. Therefore, every cent that is added in the way of unnecessary cost of transportation must be borne by the farmers of Western Canada, and if you can reduce that cost you put just that much into the pants pockets, or into the treasury, which is the same thing, of our farmers. At present we are exporting anywhere from 160,000,000 to 200,000,000 bushels a year. That would mean a saving of from $5,000,000 to $10,000,000 a year.
But does that state the whole case? Far from it. Even if a start were made on this project now, it would be from 3 to 5 years *before it would be completed and if the progress of Western Canada continues at the same rate as in the past few years, we shall be producing in Western Canada before these canals are completed anywhere from 300,000,000 to 500,000,000 bushels for export. There is no question about that. Do not think for one minute that Western Canada has ceased to progress; do not think for one minute that we have stopped our development. We have no intention of doing anything of the kind. My candid opinion is that within twenty years Saskatchewan will be the most populous

province in the Dominion. At any rate by the time the project -is completed we will have at least 400,000,000 bushels a year for export, and what an enormous profit this project will mean,-not only in cash,- for at the present time a great deal of our very superior wheat goes to Buffalo, is transported from there to New York, and, I am sorry to say, my information is that very inferior wheat is mixed with it and the mixture is then sold on the British market. Somebody makes an enormous profit out of that transaction on the American side. If we could get our grain straight on to the British market, we would prevent anything of that kind. Our good Canadian wheat would get on to the British market as good Canadian grown wheat, and our people would get the full benefit of raising grain superior to any grown anywhere else on the continent of America. It is these reasons that have induced me to support this scheme and the Hudson Bay Railway, so that we can get away from this foreign interference with our wheat.
As has been stated, this project has been supported very strongly in the United States, and lately it has been receiving very great support in our part of the country. I have before me a list of sixteen states, each of which is contributing $10,000 a year, making a total of $160,000 for propaganda work in favour of this project. They are as follows:	Illinois, Michigan,
Wisconsin, Minnesota, Indiana, Ohio, Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, Nebraska, Missouri, and one other which I cannot recall at the moment. All these sixteen states are supporting the project, backed up by a large part of the population of Western Canada. We do not intdnd to allow selfish interests anywhere to interfere with our determination to develop our country in such a way as to give to our people the full value of everything they produce and for that reason I am satisfied that this project will be started some time, and the Government might just as well make up their minds to get into the procession and take the credit for having started it.
I merely rose to give my support to this proposal, feeling that somebody from west of the Great Lakes should speak in support of it.
Mr. HENRI E. LAVIGUEUR (Quebec County) :	The project which has been
brought before the House by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) is one of great importance. I listened with great

interest to the speech of the hon. gentleman and I think that the proposal is certainly one that merits the attention of the House and of the country at large. If, however,
I may be permitted to offer the hon. gentleman a suggestion, I think that he might add to his resolution that the Committee to be selected from among the members of this House be empowered to investigate the question of grain traffic by waterways and also by way of rail. There is no doubt that this project is one of great importance, and it was really a revelation, at least to some of the members of this House, to hear the hon. gentleman state, and confirm his assertion with official figures, that over two-thirds of the grain from the west of the Great Lakes was shipped by way of Amer-ipan seaports at a cost of from five to ten cents per bushel more than it would cost by water-way from the Lakes down to the St. Lawrence. I am sure that if an investigation were held in regard to the shipment of grain by rail from Toronto to the American seaports it would be found that a further additional cost, to say nothing of loss of time, could be obviated by shipping the grain by way of the Transcontinental direct from Winnipeg to Quebec. This would represent a great economy, if we take into consideration the great advantages that could be derived from this means of transportation.
It is not too much to say that the great national port of this country, Quebec, would, if some money were spent on it to provide proper equipment, be beneficial to the whole country. I do not think that I am pessimistic in saying that at present Quebec stands in need of improvement in this respect. I believe that if the port of Quebec were adequately equipped the bulk of navigation could be concentrated there and the accruing advantage would be great. If this committee that is to be appointed to investigate the proposal before the House undertook to study the needs of Quebec I am sure that it would decide to recommend to the Government that proper equipment be provided and that adequate steps be taken to take care of grain transportation from the West direct to Quebec. I principally desired to urge upon the hon. member for Port Arthur, that he add to his resolution a clause empowering the investigation by the committee of the question of grain transportation by rail.

speechtext:
In a great movement such as this it is necessary first of all to have, in any country but especially in Canada, men of vision
and optimism who constantly advocate their views and bring them before the people until their proposals become accomplished facts. In the old days of the '20's people regarded the Welland canal as something only to be hoped for, and it would not have materialized had it not been for the special efforts of William Hamilton Merritt and George Keefer. It is a significant' and interesting fact that we have in this House now a descendant of George Keefer who is advocating as mover of this resolution, for the benefit of the country, an improvement of very much greater magnitude. Coming from the head of the Lakes he, along with my hon. friend, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), supports this proposal; and it is only proper that I, representing people at the foot of the Lakes, should also say that he will have on lake Ontario an almost unanimous assent to the project. Indeed, it has been so well thought over by the people of Toronto that they have anticipated the movement, and are not dismayed by engineering or financial obstacles. They have spent millions of dollars, and propose to send twenty million dollars and more, for the improvement of their own harbour by making it a thirty-foot harbour with dockage facilities for the ships which they hope and believe will eventually come from the ocean to increase the commerce between them and the old countries. It is true we do not expect so much benefit from what comes from the West; but if it is accomplished we shall have a harbour that will accommodate all the shipping that will come either way. Having spent this vast sum of money, with certain assistance from the Dominion, it is natural that we should desire in Toronto to see this work carried along. I know that in a matter of this sort there is always jealousy of waterborne traffic on the part of the railways. But I am convinced from what I have read on the subject that this jealousy is altogether unwarrantable. When waterborne traffic increases, the business of the railways increase at the same time. The one helps the other, and if it should turn out that there is any opposition or any coldness from the friends of the railways in regard to this scheme, I am sure that a consideration of the examples both in America and in England will dispel such opposition and show that it is unfounded in view of the facts of history.

When the Manchester Ship canal was constructed it took a great many years for the British parliament to put the project through, largely owing to the opposition of the railways. But Manchester was put upon the seas, so to speak; and yet it increased in railway traffic from Liverpool, and this vastly beyond the expectations of all concerned. The railway earnings were largely increased. The same thing will probably apply in this case. This is but a motion for a committee, and until we have that committee we cannot know where we stand. At any rate, the project is big enough and can be limited only by money and engineering consideration. We have been told on most excellent authority in the United States that this is by no means an insurmountable project financially, especially if by friendly arrangement we can be assisted by American capital. And from the engineering standpoint there is no great obstacle. It is true we are dismayed at present at the thought of spending money. But if, as my hon. friend from Fort Arthur (Mr. Keefer) pointed out, the profit will eventually be very great, and if prominent engineers, whom we cannot ignore, are of the opinion that the scheme is practicable, we can proceed, call these engineers before the committee, get something definite as to what the cost will be and a sound opinion regarding its feasibility and for the first time place before the country the engineering and financial data.
I am also impressed with the importance of the scheme from the fact that it gives an immense increase in Hydro-electrical power. On the St. Lawrence rapids, where there is a fall of 92 feet, it is estimated that we can get as much power as we now get from Niagara, and as the country on the St. Lawrence is by no means at its hayday yet it will naturally become a thriving manufacturing centre by reason of the adjacency of this power. It has been estimated by a man of eminence in the engineering field that there can be collected from tolls for electric power in the St. Lawrence valley and adjacently at least $12,000,000 a year. That sum at five per cent would represent a capitalization of $240,000,000. I do not think the scheme could be put through for $100,000,000 as has been estimated-$300,-000,000 would be a more likely figure. But if we could make it pay by developing hydraulic power through its medium and could raise an income as has been esti-

mated, namely $12,000,000 we have almost the whole cost of the work financed already, and the rest would be easy enough. The whole thing is something that appeals to every patriotic man. Water borne traffic is absolutely necessary, as we all know, to a successful country. The canals of the older countries, both in Europe and in Great Britain, have proved of immense importance; and the improvement in the building of small ocean going vessels, constructed of steel leads us to believe that it is not a chimerical idea that we should have the Great Lakes tributary to the ocean, and would have indeed a waterway that could be used with facility by all ocean going vessels except those of the very largest type. If this is so we need not be dismayed about the expenditure initially of a large sum which we can readily see will return to us at no very, distant date.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac) : Naturally I would be in favour of anything that would make for the development of Canada. For that reason I believe I would be inclined to support the resolution of my hon. friend from Port Arthur if there were not a better project, entirely through Canadian territory, capable of more easy development. The Georgian Bay Canal, rather than the St. Lawrence deep waterways would develop Canadian territory entirely for the advantage of the Canadian people. On the other hand my hon. friend in speaking of the advantages that would accure to the country from the development that he proposes said, if I caught him aright, that it would be of great benefit to the cities of Buffalo, Clev-land, Toledo, Detroit and Chicago. Now none of these cities are within the borders of Canada. A few years ago when hon. gentlemen on this side wanted a little closer trade relationship with the American people my hon. friends opposite would not have any truck or trade with them. Now they are willing to develop Canadian water courses and Canadian water powers for the benefit of Buffalo, Clevland, Toledo, Detroit and Chicago. I would very much rather, Mr. Speaker, see the Georgian Bay Canal developed, and build up such towns as North Bay, Mattawa, Pembroke, Campbell's Bay, Arnprior, Ottawa, and Hawkes-bury. These are all Canadian towns that would be developed by the Georgian Bay project. That project would also develop a country that is rich in low grade minerals, rich in agricultural possibilities, just as rich in waterway possibilities as the St.

Lawrence route, and rich in timber resources. If the Georgian Bay Canal were constructed it would be entirely through Canadian territory, and would develop Canada to a very much larger extent than would be possible by aiding the St. Lawrence route. It is true that the latter enterprise would be of greater advantage to a portion of Ontario adjacent to the St. Lawrence; but it would not be of any particular advantage to the rest of the Dominion that would not be equally benefited by the Georgian Bay Canal. The latter project would be in the interest of the greater portion of the country, it would develop the interior of Canada, and would altogether be a very much better project than the deepening of the St. Lawrence. I have not much confidence in the possibility of the deepening of the St. Lawrence at the present time when we are called upon to vote $165,000,000 to bolster up our transportation system. Mr. Sanford Evans was engaged on a report of the Georgian Bay Canal route for some two or three years; but that gentleman's report never having been presented, it does not seem that the Government are very much interested in the development of the waterways of this country. Otherwise they would have at least made public Mr. Sanford Evans' report on the Georgian Bay Canal project. Furthermore I understand that private enterprise is willing to undertake the construction of the Georgian Bay Canal. I understand there is a company that is quite willing to undertake the construction of this work and make it possible to move grain from the great West, and move to inland points coal brought from the Eastern Provinces, at no cost whatever to the taxpayers of the Dominion. If that be the case I do not see the force of my hon. friend's argument in asking for a commission to spend more money investigating the St. Lawrence route, when the Government have already in their possession reports giving full details as to the construction of the Georgian Bay Canal.
