speechtext:
I have just one or two observations to make on the resolution before the House. I listened with interest to the remarks made by my hon. friend from Port ' Arthur (Mr. Keefer) arid to the rest of the discussion that has taken place. I listened particularly to my hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) and if I gathered aright the sense of his observations he proposed to make the National Railway System pay by another
vast expenditure of money to deepen our waterways. Well, that proposition may have some merit, but I have grave doubts about it. It does strike me, Sir, in connection with this whole matter that we should have a little regard to the financial position of the country at the present time My hon. friend (Mr. Keefer) proposes t< have a commission of inquiry that I pre sume will travel round the country ant gather evidence wherever it can be gathered, sit during the recess of Parliament, and undoubtedly spend some money. I do not wish to be considered as opposing the principle of the scheme. I am among those who believe that this country would have been very much further ahead if we had spent a few of the hundreds of millions of dollars which have been expended on railways in providing this deep waterway. But we did not do so, and I do submit now that until we get our financial house in good order this is not the time to consider additional expenditures of public money on a large scale.
I am not so certain that the bringing of ocean-going vessels to the Head of the Lakes will achieve all that is expected or hoped for in the reduction of rates on grain to Europe. One very important factor which must be taken into consideration in any survey of the matter is the ocean rates from the Atlantic seaboard to Europe. It is a well established principle that ocean rates from America to Europe depend in a very considerably degree on the amount of goods that are carried from Europe to America. In other words, a vessel operating on the high seas must have a cargo both ways if it is to establish a fair rate one way. We also know that to-day a large amount of our western wheat is going out by United States Atlantic ports. The reason is simply this, that ocean-going vessels can get return cargoes from Europe to the Atlantic seaports of the United States while they cannot get them to our Canadian Atlantic ports, and that is due to the fact that the United States Atlantic ports are supplying a population of
106.000.	000, while our Atlantic ports are supplying a population of only
8.000. 000. For that reason exporters of grain, and I speak from knowledge, can always secure from Philadelphia, Newport News, New York or Boston much better ocean rates to Europe than can be secured from Canadian ports, which is a most important consideration to be kept in mind in a consideration of this whole question.



I would suggest that this resolution might well stand for a year and then possibly the scheme could be looked into in the manner suggested by my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer). I see very little to be gained in prosecuting an inquiry at considerable public expense while we have no possibility, as far as I can see, of finding the money necessary to carry on the proposed development. In a few years when our financial difficulties have cleared away and when we have put our financial house in order, we might be open to consider such a proposition; but in the meantime I would suggest that no very great harm will come if the proposal is allowed to stand over for another year.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself with the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer), not as a partisan either of the route proposed by him or of the route proposed by the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) and the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill),-the	Georgian Bay	canal

because I at once confess that I am not in a position to say which of the two is the more advantageous. But as one who is interested in the whole question of transportation, I believe that the subject brought before the House by the hon. member for Port Arthur is deserving of very careful consideration.
I do not quite agree with my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) that it is too early to begin an investigation of which is the proper route and what is the best method of relieving the country of some of the burdens it is carrying on account of the tremendous transportation charges that now obtain. As I view the situation, if Canada is to develop in competition with other countries-and she has tremendous latent resources awaiting development-it will only be by means of making transportation easier and cheaper, so that our resources may be transported from the interior of the country to the markets of the world at less cost than is possible at the present time. Transportation cost is to a very considerable extent strangling the whole progress of this country, and will continue to strangle it until we find means of cheapening the cost.
The question of the deficit on the Canadian National railways has been referred to. My judgment is that the development of our waterways will not injure our railways in the least, but rather that the in-

creased prosperity resulting from that development will make it possible to so increase the freight traffic of those railways that their revenues will be more than sufficient to cover their operating costs.
A point that in my opinion cannot be emphasized too strongly is that by making it possible for ocean-going vessels to run from Nova Scotia ports, or from England if you will, to the very centre of Canada two results will be at once achieved. First it will put us in a much more independant position than we are in at present; and. secondly, it will cheapen industry and make it possible as a consequence for Canada tc get what she must always have, a supply of reasonably cheap coal. Then there is the question of electrical development that will accrue in connection with the deepening of our waterways. It is said that there is enough electrical energy going to waste on the St. Lawrence to operate every single line of railway in Ontario and save the tremendous quantity of coal that now has to be used for that purpose. The steady increase in the cost of fuel is one of the difficulties' that our railways have to contend with. These two things would go hand in hand with either of the projects. As I said, I am not a partisan of either, and we should endeavour to find out accurately and beyond question which is the better scheme and go ahead with it. As has been pointed out, it will take time to get this under way, and if we start an investigation this year it will be one or two years before we are in a position to spend a dollar on which ever route may be chosen. I believe that the resolution is along the right lines and that the House should give it concurrence.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals) :
subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this resolution before it is finally disposed of. The transportation question is one of the most important for the future of Canada. This project has been before the country for some little time, having originated, I think, in connection with the development of the Northwest. The western provinces are, in my opinion, probably the most important factors in connection with our national development, and it is absolutely necessary that their development should be encouraged in the interests of the Dominion generally, and to ensure that development we must give them the cheapest transportation possible. It was considered in the interests of the West that we should enlarge the Welland canal, which resulted in

reducing the cost of transportation of the products of the great West to the seaboard by several cents per bushel. Later it was considered that if the St. Lawrence route also was developed the cost of transportation of the products of the West would be further decreased. The matter was brought to the attention of, and was considered by the Government, as it had been by previous governments. Later the question of the development of water-powers and of electrical energy was considered in that connection. I think it is in the interest of Canada that every possible chance of decreasing the cost of transportation, whether by the St. Lawrence route, the Georgian Bay route or the Hudson Bay route, should be considered and taken advantage of, if it is going to assist in the development of the great natural resources of Canada. When the matter was brought to the attention of this Government they took it up with the government of the United States. I would like to read a letter which was addressed to Mr. C. A. Magrath, Chairman of the International Joint Commission, as showing that the Government are alive to the situation and that they have already taken steps to ascertain exactly what the conditions are and what they would be if these routes were developed. The letter is dated at Ottawa, January 21, 1920, and is as follows:
C A. Magrath, Esq.,
Chairman, Canadian Section,
International Joint Commission,
Ottawa.
Sir,-I have the honour to inform you that the Governments of the United States of America and of the Dominion of Canada, under the provisions of Article IX of the Treaty of the 11th of January, 1909, between the Governments of the United States and Great Britain, herewith refer certain questions, as set forth below involving- the beneficial use < of the waters of th'e St. Lawrence river, between Montreal and Lake Ontario, in the interests of both countries, and, in general, the rights, obligations, or interests of either in relation to the other, or to the inhabitants of the other along their common frontier.
It is desired that the said questions be made the basis of an investigation to be carried out by the International Joint Commission, to the end that the said Commission may submit a report to the two countries covering the subject matter of this reference, together with such conclusions and recommendations as may be considered pertinent in the premises.
Question 1.

What further improvement in the St. Lawrence River, between Montreal and Lake Ontario, is necessary to make the same navigable for deep draught vessels of either the lake or ocean-going type; what draught of water is recommended, and what is the estimated cost?
In answering this question the Commission is requested to consider:
(a)	Navigation interests alone, whether by the construction of locks and dams in the river; by side canals with the necessary locks; or by a combination of the two.
(b)	The combination of navigation and power interests to obtain the greatest beneficial use of the waters of the river.
Question 2.-Which of the schemes submitted by the Government or other engineers is preferred, and why?
Question 3.-Under what general method of procedure and in what general order shall the various physical and administrative features of the improvement be carried out?
Question 4.-Upon what basis shall the capital cost of the completed improvement be apportioned to each country?
Question 5.-Upon what basiis shall the costs of operation and maintenance be apportioned to each country?	-
Question 6.-What method of control is recommended for the operation of the improved waterway to secure its most beneficial use?
Question 7.-Will regulating Lake Ontario increase the low water flow in the St. Lawrence ship channel below Montreal? And if so, to what extent and at what additional cost?
Question 8.-To what extent will the improvement develop the resources, commerce and industry of each country?
Question 9.-What traffic, both incoming and outgoing, in kind and quantity, is likely to be carried upon the proposed route both at its inception and in the future? Consideration to be given not only to present conditions, but to probable changes therein resulting from the development of industrial activities due to availability of large quantities of hydraulic power?
Pending the receipt of plans, estimates, and other engineering data necessary for the final consideration of this reference, the Commission is requested to hold such public hearings as may be considered necessary or advisable in order to obtain all information bearing, directly or indirectly, on the physical, commercial and economic feasibility of the project as a whole.
To facilitate the preparation of the desired report each Government will, from its official engineering personnel appoint an engineer with full authority to confer with a similar officer of the other Government for the purpose: first, of acquiring, each in his own country, such data as may be found necessary to supplement the existing engineering data and surveys, and second, of preparing complete outline plans for and estimates of the cost of the proposed improvement, including the value of all property easements, damages and rights connected therewith. These plans and estimates are to be submitted to the Commission as soon as practicable but not later than one year from the date of appointment and the Commission is requested to forward to the two Governments its final report with recommendation not later than three months thereafter. A copy of the instructions furnished these engineers is attached hereto.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Tour obedient servant.
N. W. Rowell,
Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs.
So that over a year ago the Government took action in this matter. The United States government agreed, in accordance with the subject matter of this letter, to a reference of the whole question to the

International Joint Commission. That commission has held hearings in the United States and in Canada, and its report will be presented to each government in due course. The matter had to he brought before both governments because the St. Lawrence river is, in part, an international waterway and the consent of both governments would have to be obtained before we could proceed with any such development as is advocated in this resolution.
I know the St. Lawrence waterways route. There are at present twenty-six locks between the upper entrance of the river St. Lawrence and the city of Montreal. There is a fourteen foot draught for vessels passing through that waterway. If five dams were constructed we would have a waterway through which any vessel could pass that crosses the Atlantic and such vessels would be able to proceed to Port Arthur when the Welland canal is completed. In the construction of these five dams,* at least two million horse-power would be developed. In my opinion, once the Welland canal is completed, it will be almost absolutely necessary that the St. Lawrence waterway should be proceeded with and, if financial conditions will allow, that it should be completed. I believe the development of the St. Lawrence waterway would decrease the cost of transportation by several cents per bushel on all grain produced in the western provinces, but I feel that the development of this waterway is also of very great importance to Ontario and part of Quebec as well, in another way.
Every year the people of Ontario, yes, and I may say part of Manitoba, are in fear and trembling on account of coal strikes taking place on the other side of the line, because, when strikes occur, it is almost impossible to secure coal. If we had the St. Lawrence waterway completed, we would be able to bring coal from Nova Scotia to that part of Quebec that is on the St. Lawrence river west of Montreal, also to Ontario up to Port Arthur and even as far as Winnipeg, thus saving a recurrence of the fear and trembling that we have had in the past on account of the possibility of a shortage of fuel during the winter months.
Some hon. gentlemen have referred to the Georgian Bay route, and while I do not wish to take issue with them in regard to that route, I wish to draw their attention to the fact, that vessels that would cross the Atlantic could not possibly make use of the Georgian Bay route. Vessels
TMr. J. D. Reid.]
that would pass through the St. Lawrence canal and through the Welland canal and on to Port Arthur would be vessels of
12,000,	15,000 or 18,000 tons. The route along the Georgian Bay canal is narrow, and vessels of that type could not possibly go through that canal. There is no doubt that there would be a large development of waterpower if the Georgian Bay canal were proceeded with, but it would not take the place of our great St. Lawrence Canal route. Private parties, I believe, would build the five dams along the St. Lawrence river if we would give them the water-powers, but I am one of those who do not believe it is in the public interest to hand over our natural resources, such as two or three million horse-power to private parties to develop. They should be held in the public interest, but I mention that to show the House that the development of the great water-powers on the St. Lawrence would almost pay for the investment that would have to be made for carrying out this great project.
It has also been mentioned that a large proportion of our products goes via Buffalo, and there is no doubt about that. Up to the present time, each year a large percentage of the products of the great West goes via Buffalo. It should go via Montreal and our great St. Lawrence route, but it cannot go that way until we are able to compete with our transportation rates, and as long as the development of the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence route is delayed, just so long will the transshipment of grain via the St. Lawrence route be delayed.
An hon. member mentioned that this project was in the interest of Cleveland and other American ports, but that is not a fact, except in this way. Americans, at least in many of the Western States, are looking at this project in much the same way as people in Western Canada. If they can ship their products via Duluth and by the St. Lawrence route, and in that way get their products more cheaply to the European market, it is in their interest to urge their country to take part in developing this route which Americans are interested in on account of its being international.
Some hon. member has referred to the large amount that the development of our railways is costing the country, and there is no doubt that that is a very serious matter. I had not intended referring to it were it not that some hon. members mentioned it casually in the discussion this

evening. The cost of operation of railways, not only in Canada, but. in the United States, has increased so tremendously in the last two or three years that, in my judgment, it is hindering or preventing the future development of our country, and unless some means are taken to decrease the cost of operation of our railways, the development of our country will continue to be hindered. The development of this country and the United States has been hindered by what is called the McAdoo award in fixing the wages of railway employees. Some action must be taken, and I think the railway employees themselves should look into this matter and endeavour to adjust matters in such a way that the future of this country will not be hindered on account of the enormous cost of operation of railways as is the case at the present time.
The Estimates that have been presented to the House to-day, perhaps, may not and cannot be understood until we are able to explain them to the House in detail, but the fact that the sum of $160,000,000 appears in the Estimates does not mean that there has been that loss in connection with the railways, or that it is estimated there will be that loss next year. What it really means is that it has been estimated by those who are in charge of the Canadian National railways, which include the Canadian Northern, the Intercolonial, the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific, that there will be a loss of some $50,000,000 during the year 1921. But in addition to that loss, large amounts are required for construction- betterments that are really charged to capital account-and in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific a large amount will have to be charged in connection with capital account. As regards the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which the Government must take over, the Government has to assume responsibility in connection with liabilities that are falling due. It must not, however, be considered that the amount mentioned in the Estimates means a deficit of that amount next year. There is no doubt that the Canadian National railways and the other Canadian railways are meeting with great losses; but the railways in the United States are meeting with proportionately much larger losses than our Canadian railways. I mention this in passing simply for the reason that one or two speakers who have touched upon it do not, I believe, understand the situation. Otherwise, they would not
have given out the impression that the railways were losing the amounts mentioned in the Estimates.
I am myself very anxious that these great waterways should be developed, first, for navigation purposes. I believe in the development of this great waterway. I believe it would be worth the amount it would cost simply because of the development it would bring to the West from Port Arthur to British Columbia. In addition to that, I believe it would be of the greatest importance in developing the natural resources in Ontario and Quebec from Port Arthur east. I believe also it is one of the most important projects that could be undertaken for the protection of that part of the country from Manitoba east, so far as its coal and fuel supply for the future is concerned. There is the additional fact that it would develop some 2,000,000 to
3,000,000 horse power. This development would cheapen the cost of transportation on the railways between Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa. It would furnish power for a very large number of industries in Ontario and elsewhere in Canada, and would assist in the development of the natural resources of this province and Canada generally. It would mean the bringing of more people to Ontario and Canada. Population is what we want, and everything should be done towards that end. As Minister of Railways I have hesitated to urge proceeding with this work during the last two or three years, on account of the very great expenditures due to the war, and also on account of the large amounts that are required to complete at the very earliest possible date projects that have already been undertaken.
So far as this resolution is concerned I do not think it would be advisable to appoint a Special Committee while the present Waterways Commission is investigating this question.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
But I believe it would be in the interests of Canada as a whole that hon. members of this House should have the opportunity of learning just what this waterway means towards the development of the West, of Central Canada, and of the country as a whole. Having already referred this matter to the International Joint Waterways Commission, I would suggest to the hon. member that if he can see his way clear to withdraw his resolution, I would undertake to have it brought before the committee of this House which has

already been constituted, consisting of some 30 or 35 members, and known as the Forest Waterways and Water Powers Committee, with a view to having the committee take whatever steps they think necessary to secure all available information on this project. In that way we would not be interfering with the Joint Waterways Commission, and probably before Parliament prorogues the committee would have before it the final report of the Waterways Commission, and would then be in a position to bring before the House all the facts in connection with the matter, and the question could be discussed here. I am sure that when the committee has received the report of the International Joint Waterways Commission, and has collected information on its own account, its decision and that of the House will be to proceed with the development of this great waterways system, not only for navigation but for power purposes, just as soon as the financial conditions of the country will permit.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
At the risk of being considered unprogressive in the promotion of this enterprise, I feel very much inclined to agree with the leader of the Progressive party. That is perhaps all the more remarkable in view of the fact that the original movement for the development of the great waterways was launched in the city of Kitchener, or Berlin as it was then, something like eight years ago. A meeting was held there of representatives from various municipalities throughout western Ontario to develop an organization that should promote the deepening of the waterways to permit of the bringing of ocean vessels up to the head of the lakes. The result of that meeting was that a deputation of something like 1,800 or 2,000 men waited upon the Government in the House of Commons Chamber in the old building about eight years ago; but nothing particular came of it. At that time I was in favour of the development that is suggested now, because I believed it would do a great deal of good. But that was before the war, before we had laid on this country a debt of nearly two-and-a-half billion dollars. I for one do not look lightly as one hon. member did to-night, on the expenditure of a mere bagatelle of $100,000,000 at this time and which would probably expand to twice this amount before completion. I think the country ought to set its financial house in order before it takes upon itself any such heavy financial obligations as are suggested at this particular time.

Just in passing I might refer to an argument made by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan), who stated that if he felt this development would interfere with the construction of the Hudson Bay railway he would be against it. Now, Sir, that is one of the reasons, if there were any,* why I would be for it, for I believe, in regard to that particular enterprise, that this country has entered upon an expenditure which is almost entirely wasted and should not be continued. It has also been stated that the deepening of the waterway will decrease the cost of carrying wheat from the West. Probably it would do so; but I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that just to the extent to which the wheat is carried by waterway, the railways will find their business diminished. The result, I presume, would be that in order to get larger receipts and decrease the deficits on the railways we would continue again and again to increase the railway rates, and finally the latter would do a constantly lessening business and the deficit would accumulate from year to year owing to lack of traffic. I for one believe, Mr. Speaker, that the present deficit is, to some extent at least, the result of an increase in rates which makes it impossible to do business at a profit.
The Minister of Railways and Canals, (Mr. Reid) advanced another argument which is of considerable interest to those of us who come from Central Ontario where we have no coal. He believes that with the deepening of the waterways it would be possible to bring coal from the Maritime Provinces at a cheap rate and sell it in Ontario and also farther west. I think the argument is a good one; but accompanying it I believe there would, have to be a stipulation that the coal of the Maritime Provinces be taken from the control of the two great corporations which have it in their possession at this time. And I for one, speaking in the light of the history of the development of resources in this country, do not believe for one moment that, even if the cost of carrying coal were greatly reduced, the general public would benefit a great deal from such reduction so long as these great and necessary natural resources remained entirely under the control of private interests.
Now, that is all I have to say. I do not wish to be understood as being opposed to the project ultimately, but I do not think that the present is the time for entering upon the expenditure of another hundred

million dollars for this work. We should first find out where we stand, and it will be time enough to proceed with an undertaking of this nature when the Dominion of Canada has adjusted itself to the burden under which it is labouring to-day.

Coming from
the far East, Mr. Speaker, and being as you know directly and indirectly interested in this discussion, I should like to say something on the motion before the Chair. But it is now getting late, and as I understand that there are other hon. gentlemen who desire to speak on the subject, with your permission I move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to.
